anatomical_context: Oral cavity and oropharyngeal feeding apparatus, including lips, jaw, tongue, and swallowing interface.
Axial/postural and orofacial neuromuscular systems may interact during feeding, but published UNC80 reports did not anatomically partition the deficit.
The airway interface becomes relevant in cases with aspiration or possible aspiration pneumonia, without proof of the phase at which airway protection failed.
profiles.causal_role: The focal abnormality is best positioned as a functional mediator between the severe neurodevelopmental/neuromotor phenotype and downstream feeding failure: impaired suck, chew, oral transfer, or swallow can reduce oral intake and make it unsafe. Dysphagia co-occurs with aspiration or aspiration pneumonia in some reports, so impaired airway protection is a plausible downstream route, but the available cases do not isolate oral-motor dysfunction from hypotonia, appetite, reflux, respiratory control, or pharyngeal dysfunction and therefore do not prove that route.
cell_types: No specific cell type was directly assayed in the clinical feeding studies.

Orofacial motor neurons, bulbar pattern-generating circuits, sensory afferents, neuromuscular junctions, and oral/pharyngeal muscle fibers are physiologically relevant but remain unlocalized possibilities rather than established UNC80-deficiency findings.
contradictions: Severity and persistence vary: one documented dysphagia improved enough for solid food by age five, whereas another child remained gastrostomy-dependent at age eight.
The cohort described poor sucking together with little appetite in one child, demonstrating that feeding difficulty cannot automatically be attributed entirely to oral-motor failure.
Feeding difficulty is common, but published cohort counts do not report a standardized oral-motor diagnosis, so 11/12 cannot be interpreted as the prevalence of the focal mechanism itself.

distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Orobuccal dyskinesias and persistent open-mouth posture occur in some affected individuals and may disrupt oral coordination.

Possible aspiration pneumonia in one report and co-occurrence in another do not prove that oral-phase dysfunction, rather than pharyngeal, reflux, or respiratory-control abnormalities, caused airway invasion.

distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Dysphagia or difficult feeding co-occurs with recurrent aspiration or possible aspiration pneumonia in some individuals.

downstream_consequences: Feeding difficulty, texture restriction, prolonged assisted nutrition, and nasogastric or gastrostomy dependence.
Poor weight gain and failure to thrive, although appetite and other gastrointestinal or systemic contributors were not excluded.
Recurrent aspiration or aspiration pneumonia in some individuals; the specific contribution of oral-motor dysfunction remains unresolved.

established_pathology_observations.observation: In a cohort of 12 individuals with biallelic UNC80 variants, feeding difficulties were reported in 11/12, hypotonia in 10/12, and extrapyramidal or abnormal movements in 8/12.
One infant with biallelic UNC80 variants was hospitalized at one month for poor weight gain attributed to poor sucking and little appetite and continued to require small enriched meals at four years.
One affected girl had difficult feeding requiring nasogastric tube feeding together with recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
An eight-year-old with a pathogenic UNC80 variant had dysphagia with gastrostomy dependence and was admitted with possible aspiration pneumonia.
In a molecularly confirmed individual, poor sucking progressed to dysphagia requiring a semi-liquid diet, and oral intake later improved sufficiently for solid foods by age five.
Two sisters with UNC80 loss of function had early feeding impairment: one required nasogastric feeding for the first four days and the other was hypotonic and received a gastrostomy for poor feeding.

gaps: No disease-specific videofluoroscopic or fiberoptic swallow findings define oral versus pharyngeal phase impairment, silent aspiration, residue, or timing abnormalities.
No quantitative chewing, tongue-pressure, lip-seal, suck-swallow-breathe coordination, or oral-motor scale data were identified.
No study separates contributions from hypotonia, dyskinesia, appetite, gastroesophageal reflux, cognition, sensory processing, and central respiratory control.
No genotype-severity analysis or longitudinal natural-history estimate exists specifically for oral-motor dysfunction.
No patient-derived neuronal or neuromuscular model directly connects UNC80/NALCN-channel dysfunction to oropharyngeal motor performance.
mechanisms: Reduced suck and oral bolus-control performance is directly described by poor sucking and progression to dysphagia.

Generalized or axial hypotonia is a plausible contributor to reduced orofacial force and postural control because it commonly co-occurs with feeding difficulty, but disease reports did not measure oral-muscle strength or demonstrate mediation.
Orobuccal dyskinesias, persistent open-mouth posture, and broader abnormal movements may add a coordination defect in some individuals; their contribution to swallowing was not quantified.

Impaired swallowing or airway protection may connect the focal deficit to aspiration, but case-level co-occurrence does not distinguish oral-phase, pharyngeal-phase, central-respiratory, or reflux-related mechanisms.
profiles.normal_state: Normal oral feeding requires coordinated orofacial sensorimotor sequencing: effective suck or chew, bolus preparation and oral transfer, timely swallow initiation, and coordination with airway protection. This normal-state description is physiological inference used to interpret the reported poor sucking, dysphagia, and oral-coordination deficit; it was not directly measured in the UNC80 reports.
profiles.pathological_state: In affected individuals, oral feeding performance is reduced: sucking may be poor from infancy, chewing/swallowing/oral coordination may be impaired, and dysphagia can require modified textures or enteral feeding. Persistently open-mouth posture and orobuccal dyskinesias in some individuals suggest additional motor-control abnormalities, but neither is established as universal or as the sole cause of dysphagia.
profiles.summary: Oral-motor dysfunction in UNC80 deficiency is a clinically described impairment of sucking, chewing, swallowing, and oral coordination. The disease-specific record includes poor sucking from early infancy, dysphagia, texture restriction, nasogastric or gastrostomy dependence, and difficult feeding; a 12-person biallelic-UNC80 cohort reported feeding difficulty in 11/12 and hypotonia in 10/12. These observations establish a clinically important feeding-function abnormality, but the published studies do not provide instrumental swallow physiology, oral-force measurements, or a disease-specific cellular mechanism.
temporal_context: Onset can be neonatal or early-infantile, documented as need for nasogastric feeding, lethargy during feeds, or poor sucking.
The course is variable: one individual progressed from poor sucking to dysphagia and later managed solid food by age five, while another remained gastrostomy-dependent with dysphagia at age eight.
Cohort reports are cross-sectional and do not establish whether oral-motor function is static, developmentally delayed, fluctuating, or progressive across the disorder.
profiles.uncertainty: Evidence is human and disease-specific but predominantly retrospective, case-level, and based on unstandardized clinical labels. Poor sucking and dysphagia directly establish abnormal feeding function; attribution to a particular oral muscle, neural circuit, swallow phase, or molecular mechanism is inference. Tube dependence and aspiration are severity/consequence markers, not specific assays of oral-motor dysfunction. The curation boundary is therefore preserved: appetite, gastric transit, aspiration, respiratory infection, generalized hypotonia, and dyskinesia are related but separable processes.
upstream_causes: Biallelic UNC80 loss of function is the disease context in the molecularly confirmed cohorts, but a direct molecular-to-oral-motor causal chain has not been experimentally demonstrated.
Generalized or axial hypotonia is a plausible contributor based on frequent co-occurrence.
Orobuccal dyskinesia or broader abnormal movements may independently impair coordination in a subset.
Severe neurodevelopmental impairment could disrupt learned sensorimotor feeding sequences, but this was not directly tested.

profiles.causal_role: This is a proximal biochemical consequence of UNC80 loss that links genotype to several separable downstream states. The strongest causal evidence comes from knockout and knock-in mouse neurons, heterologous interaction assays, and reconstituted structural-functional systems. The complex defect can reduce UNC79 stability or recruitment, membrane localization, channel regulation, and neuronal sodium-leak current; transfer of the exact quantitative chain to human UNC80-deficient neurons remains untested.

Mouse brain neurons represented in whole-brain membrane and protein preparations

contradictions: Complex destabilization does not mean total disappearance of NALCN: total NALCN protein was comparable in UNC80-null and wild-type mouse brain, and raising NALCN expression increased residual leak current without UNC80.

UNC80-null mouse neurons retained some basal NALCN conductance, and a disease-associated C-terminal truncation supported whole-cell current despite failed dendritic localization and UNC79 recruitment. Thus whole-cell current, spatial localization, and complex composition are separable readouts.

A reconstituted four-subunit system found UNC79 and UNC80 essential for robust current and for surface localization/gating, whereas mouse hippocampal neurons can retain basal NALCN current without either auxiliary subunit. This likely reflects assay, cell-type, and endpoint differences rather than a single all-or-none requirement.

UNC79 protein was drastically reduced in complete UNC80 knockout but remained at wild-type-like levels in the L2654* C-terminal truncation despite loss of the mapped strong UNC79-binding region, indicating that the mapped interaction is not the sole determinant of UNC79 stability.

distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: UNC80-null mouse hippocampal neurons retain some NALCN-dependent conductance but have a drastically smaller leak current and no obvious potentiation when extracellular calcium is lowered.

distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: The UNC79-UNC80 heterodimer binds three cytoplasmic-loop motifs of NALCN; two contacts support plasma-membrane localization and another displaces an autoinhibitory helix from the NALCN C-terminal domain.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Loss of the UNC79-UNC80 assembly is predicted from direct reconstitution perturbations to reduce NALCN surface localization and leave more channels in an autoinhibited configuration.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A structurally resolved downstream mechanism by which focal complex under-assembly can impair channel function; no separate curated node covers both contacts and gating release.

established_pathology_observations.observation: UNC80-null mouse brain had drastically reduced UNC79 protein despite comparable total NALCN protein, and cultured UNC80-null hippocampal neurons had markedly smaller NALCN-dependent sodium-leak current with no clear potentiation after lowering extracellular calcium.

A mouse C-terminal truncation corresponding to a human disease-associated UNC80 truncation retained NALCN protein and whole-cell current but lost UNC79 association with the NALCN complex and lacked normal dendritic localization.
A disease-associated UNC80 interaction-domain missense substitution tested in a heterologous co-immunoprecipitation assay reduced apparent UNC80-UNC79 affinity by approximately 60 percent.

gaps: No study directly measures NALCN complex stoichiometry, surface abundance, current, resting membrane potential, or excitability in patient-derived neurons carrying biallelic UNC80 variants.
The allele-by-allele relationship among UNC80 protein abundance, UNC79 stability, channelosome assembly, subcellular localization, and clinical severity is unresolved.
The degradation machinery and turnover rates responsible for reciprocal UNC79-UNC80 protein dependence are unknown.
Cell-type specificity across human excitatory, inhibitory, autonomic, respiratory-rhythm, and peripheral neurons has not been mapped.
The quantitative contribution of impaired surface localization versus altered gating versus loss of calcium-dependent regulation is unknown in vivo.
It remains unclear whether FAM155A and FAM155B usage or additional channelosome partners modify the assembly defect in relevant human neuronal populations.
mechanisms: UNC80 directly serves as the intermediary scaffold by associating with NALCN and with UNC79, enabling UNC79 recruitment into the channelosome.
UNC79 and UNC80 show reciprocal protein-level dependence in knockout brain, so loss of one auxiliary component can destabilize the other without eliminating total NALCN protein.
Multiple contacts between the UNC79-UNC80 heterodimer and NALCN cytoplasmic loops support channel surface localization and relieve a NALCN autoinhibitory interaction.

Loss of UNC80 reduces NALCN-dependent sodium-leak current and abolishes extracellular-calcium responsiveness in mouse hippocampal neurons, connecting the assembly defect to altered membrane-potential control.

Disease-associated UNC80 C-terminal variants can selectively weaken UNC79 binding and dendritic localization while sparing residual or even robust whole-cell NALCN current, showing that functional consequences depend on the affected domain.
profiles.normal_state: At neuronal membranes, NALCN and FAM155A form the pore-containing subcomplex while the cytosolic UNC79-UNC80 heterodimer is tethered through multiple NALCN cytoplasmic-loop contacts. UNC80 contacts both NALCN and UNC79; these contacts stabilize or recruit UNC79, support surface localization, relieve an autoinhibitory NALCN interaction, and permit robust and regulated sodium-leak conductance.
profiles.pathological_state: Loss-of-function UNC80 alleles remove or weaken the scaffold in a domain-dependent manner. In UNC80-null mouse brain, UNC79 protein is drastically reduced while NALCN protein remains detectable; cultured UNC80-null hippocampal neurons have a markedly smaller NALCN-dependent sodium-leak current and lose its potentiation by low extracellular calcium. C-terminal disease-associated truncation can preserve whole-cell current yet abolish UNC79 recruitment into the NALCN complex and dendritic localization, while a disease-associated interaction-domain missense change reduces apparent UNC80-UNC79 affinity.
profiles.summary: UNC80 is a central intracellular scaffold and auxiliary subunit of the neuronal NALCN channelosome. It participates in the UNC79-UNC80 heterodimer, connects that scaffold to NALCN, and supports channel surface localization, gating, and regulated sodium-leak current. Biallelic loss or functionally important truncation of UNC80 therefore produces a genotype- and domain-dependent failure of complex stability or assembly rather than a uniform absence of NALCN protein: UNC79 abundance or recruitment can fall, NALCN-dependent current and extracellular-calcium responsiveness can be reduced, and dendritic localization can fail even when residual whole-cell current persists.

Neonatal period, when complete mouse UNC80 loss causes apnea and lethality
Ongoing mature-neuron membrane-potential regulation, inferred from cultured hippocampal-neuron electrophysiology
profiles.uncertainty: The focal state is well supported as a proximal molecular mechanism, but its magnitude and composition are allele- and assay-dependent. Complete UNC80 knockout destabilizes UNC79 and reduces regulated NALCN current in mouse neurons, while selected C-terminal variants uncouple dendritic localization and UNC79 recruitment from whole-cell current. Structural reconstitution establishes how the normal complex assembles but does not by itself show the exact conformation or abundance of complexes in human UNC80-deficient neurons. Claims about human membrane potential, circuit function, or clinical phenotype are therefore mechanistic inferences rather than direct human cellular observations.

profiles.causal_role: A proximal cellular-electrophysiology mechanism downstream of UNC80-dependent channel-complex assembly, localization, and regulatory coupling. Reduced or spatially misallocated NALCN conductance can change the Na+/K+ permeability balance at subthreshold potentials and alter spontaneous and stimulus-coupled firing. The link from these cellular effects to any particular human phenotype remains inferential because no patient-derived neuronal electrophysiology or compartment-resolved human recordings are available.
cell_types: mouse hippocampal neurons
mouse ventral tegmental area neurons

contradictions: The p.Pro1700Ser-equivalent UNC80 protein retained detectable binding to NALCN and UNC79 but generated significantly smaller current, showing that preserved co-immunoprecipitation does not establish functional channel regulation.

Disease-associated C-terminal truncation preserved or increased whole-cell NALCN current and surface expression in mouse/heterologous systems while causing loss of dendritic localization, loss of UNC79 recruitment, apnea, and lethality; therefore whole-cell current amplitude alone cannot represent the pathology.

Low extracellular Ca2+ was reported to excite hippocampal neurons through a CaSR/G-protein/UNC80-NALCN pathway, whereas neocortical-neuron experiments found voltage-gated Na+ channel gating was dominant and CaSR deletion did not change NALCN activation. This is a regional/model disagreement, not evidence that either mechanism is universal.

UNC80 deficiency can reduce a depolarizing leak conductance, but seizures occur in some affected individuals; the evidence does not establish a simple chain from uniformly increased or decreased single-cell excitability to seizure burden.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Subthreshold inward Na+ conductance and its contribution to resting-potential control are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: neuronal plasma membrane, demonstrated in cultured mouse hippocampal neurons; variant function also tested in HEK293T cells
distinct_mechanisms.label: Loss of basal UNC80-dependent NALCN sodium-leak current
limitations: The cited UNC80-null study quantified leak current under voltage clamp but did not directly measure resting potential in human UNC80-deficient neurons.
The sign and magnitude of firing changes depend on the other conductances expressed by each neuron.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC80 potentiates a small TTX-resistant NALCN-mediated inward Na+ current at subthreshold neuronal membrane potentials.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: UNC80 knockout or function-reducing variants markedly reduce the measurable NALCN-dependent Na+ leak current.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Core electrophysiological defect contained within the focal identity.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Functional membrane-channel abundance and/or probability of opening are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: neuronal and heterologous-cell plasma membrane
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced NALCN surface delivery and current potentiation
limitations: The indexed node is based on axonal NCA-1 localization in C. elegans, whereas surface-expression experiments used mammalian cells.
The non-trafficking component of UNC80-mediated current potentiation remains mechanistically unresolved.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC80 increases surface NALCN and potentiates current beyond the effect explained by surface abundance alone.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Loss of UNC80 reduces functional current despite preserved total NALCN protein; the defect is not rescued by adding NALCN or UNC79 alone.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Upstream determinant of the focal subthreshold conductance; the localization component is already represented by the indexed channel-localization profile.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Dynamic modulation of NALCN current by extracellular Ca2+ is reduced or absent.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: plasma membrane of cultured mouse hippocampal neurons
distinct_mechanisms.label: Failure of extracellular-Ca2+-dependent NALCN regulation
limitations: A later neocortical-neuron study found that voltage-gated Na+ channel gating, not NALCN, dominated low-divalent excitability and that CaSR deletion did not alter NALCN activation.
The relative roles of direct Ca2+ effects, CaSR/G proteins, and cell-type-specific conductances remain unresolved.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: In cultured hippocampal neurons, reducing extracellular Ca2+ increases NALCN-dependent Na+ leak through a pathway reported to require CaSR, G proteins, UNC80, UNC79, and the NALCN C terminus.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Without UNC80 or an intact complex, NALCN current loses potentiation by low extracellular Ca2+, reducing one route by which ionic context changes excitability.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A context-sensitive regulatory component of the focal membrane-potential-control identity.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Neuromodulator-evoked inward cation current and slow excitation are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: mouse hippocampal and ventral tegmental neurons
distinct_mechanisms.label: Loss of neuropeptide/Src-coupled slow excitation
limitations: No patient-neuron experiment has measured substance P or neurotensin responses.
The pathway was demonstrated acutely in mouse neurons and reconstituted cells.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Substance P and neurotensin activate NALCN-containing currents in mouse hippocampal and ventral tegmental neurons; substance-P coupling requires UNC80 and Src-family kinases but not G-protein activation.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: UNC80 dysfunction is expected to weaken or uncouple this NALCN-mediated slow-excitatory response.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A regulated excitability component within the focal identity; the pathological direction in UNC80-deficient human neurons is an inference from the requirement for UNC80 in the experimental system.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Spatial control of subthreshold conductance in dendrites is reduced despite preserved somatic whole-cell current.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: soma and dendrites of cultured mouse hippocampal neurons
distinct_mechanisms.label: Compartment-specific loss of dendritic UNC80-NALCN regulation
limitations: Direct dendritic membrane-potential recordings were not performed.
The indexed profile concerns truncated UNC80 trafficking, and variant-general transfer is not established.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: The UNC80 C terminus overcomes a soma-retention signal, enables dendritic localization, and recruits UNC79 to the NALCN complex.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Disease-associated C-terminal truncation can preserve or increase whole-cell NALCN current and surface expression while eliminating dendritic UNC80 localization and UNC79 recruitment.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: An upstream spatial determinant of the focal electrophysiological control variable, already covered by the indexed UNC80-trafficking profile.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Spatial propagation and synaptic-region activity are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans neuronal cell bodies, axons, synaptic regions, and neuromuscular junctions
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced propagation of neuronal activity to synaptic regions
limitations: The result is from NCA loss in C. elegans and has not been directly reproduced in human UNC80-deficient neurons.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: In C. elegans, the NCA/UNC-79/UNC-80 system supports transmission of depolarizing activity from neuronal cell bodies toward synaptic regions.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: NCA loss leaves somatic calcium activity relatively intact while reducing synaptic calcium transients and neuromuscular transmission.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A downstream consequence of disturbed membrane-potential control that is independently represented in the curated index.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Complex stability, subunit recruitment, and functional regulatory competence are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: NALCN-UNC79-UNC80 complex at neuronal membranes
distinct_mechanisms.label: Loss of UNC80-mediated NALCN-complex assembly and regulatory competence
limitations: Physical association alone is not sufficient for normal current, as shown by p.Pro1700Ser-equivalent UNC80.
The relative contribution of assembly, trafficking, and gating varies by variant.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC80 binds NALCN and UNC79, supports normal UNC79 protein abundance, and makes the complex competent for regulated current.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: UNC80 loss reduces UNC79 abundance and removes normal NALCN-current potentiation; some missense variants preserve binding yet reduce current, while C-terminal truncation abolishes UNC79 recruitment.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: An upstream mechanism already covered by the indexed NALCN-complex-destabilization profile; retained here only to locate the focal electrophysiological defect in its causal chain.

downstream_consequences: Inference: altered Na+/K+ permeability balance at subthreshold potentials and impaired stabilization of cell-specific resting membrane potential
Reduced spontaneous or modulator-evoked firing in neuronal contexts where NALCN is a major depolarizing conductance
Compartment-specific loss of dendritic membrane-potential regulation and information integration
Reduced propagation of activity to synaptic regions and reduced synaptic transmission in the C. elegans NCA-loss model
Circuit-level outcomes can be mixed because other leak, persistent Na+, HCN, and voltage-gated conductances differ across neurons and may compensate

established_pathology_observations.observation: A disease-associated UNC80 p.Pro1700Ser-equivalent protein produced significantly smaller NALCN currents than wild-type UNC80 in transfected HEK293T cells, despite comparable protein production and retained association with NALCN and UNC79.
UNC80-null mouse hippocampal neurons showed a marked loss of TTX-resistant Na+ leak current that was restored by UNC80 cDNA but not by NALCN or UNC79 cDNA alone.
People with biallelic UNC80 variants had severe neurodevelopmental disease, but their neuronal resting membrane potential and excitability were not directly recorded.

gaps: No study identified here directly measured resting membrane potential, NALCN current, firing threshold, or spontaneous firing in patient-derived UNC80-deficient neurons.
No compartment-resolved recording has tested the proposed dendritic membrane-potential defect caused by human C-terminal UNC80 truncations.
The neuron classes and developmental stages in which UNC80 loss causes the largest functional deficit in the human brain are unknown.
The relative contributions of channel abundance, channel opening, complex stability, and subcellular localization have not been resolved for most human variants.

The contribution of CaSR/G-protein signaling versus direct extracellular-Ca2+ effects and voltage-gated Na+ channel surface-charge effects is cell-type dependent and unresolved in disease-relevant neurons.
The causal mapping from disturbed subthreshold conductance to hypotonia, intellectual disability, sleep disturbance, respiratory dysrhythmia, and seizures remains incomplete.
mechanisms: UNC80-dependent potentiation of the small TTX-resistant NALCN Na+ leak at subthreshold membrane potentials
UNC80-dependent control of NALCN surface abundance plus additional current potentiation consistent with altered channel opening or protein modification
UNC80-dependent coupling of extracellular Ca2+ changes to NALCN current, with evidence that the relative contribution is neuron-type dependent
UNC80/Src-dependent coupling of substance P and neurotensin receptors to slow NALCN-mediated excitation
Compartment-specific UNC80 localization and UNC79 recruitment needed for dendritic rather than merely somatic NALCN function
Downstream propagation of depolarizing activity toward synaptic regions in the C. elegans NCA/UNC-80 system
profiles.normal_state: At subthreshold membrane potentials, the neuronal NALCN-UNC79-UNC80 complex carries a small TTX-resistant inward Na+ leak. UNC80 increases functional NALCN current, supports surface and dendritic localization, and permits modulation by extracellular Ca2+ and by neuropeptide/Src signaling. Together with K+, HCN, persistent voltage-gated Na+, and other conductances, this provides cell- and compartment-specific control of resting potential, spontaneous firing, and responsiveness to modulators.
profiles.pathological_state: UNC80 loss or function-reducing variants diminish the magnitude and/or regulation of NALCN-dependent Na+ leak. UNC80-null mouse hippocampal neurons had delta I_LNa reduced from 12.0 +/- 1.5 pA to 2.4 +/- 0.4 pA, and a human disease-associated p.Pro1700Ser-equivalent protein produced significantly smaller NALCN currents despite preserved binding to NALCN and UNC79. C-terminal truncations can preserve whole-cell current while abolishing dendritic localization and UNC79 recruitment, showing that disturbed control includes spatial and regulatory failure rather than a single monotonic current deficit.
profiles.summary: Biallelic UNC80 dysfunction disrupts control of a small, subthreshold NALCN-mediated inward Na+ conductance that normally helps set neuronal membrane potential and couples extracellular and neuromodulatory signals to excitability. Disease-associated UNC80 variants and UNC80-null mouse hippocampal neurons show reduced NALCN current or loss of its regulation. The inferred patient-neuron consequence is impaired stabilization and context-dependent control of resting potential, not necessarily uniform hypoexcitability: effects vary by neuronal compartment, cell type, variant, and compensatory conductances, and resting potential has not been directly measured in human UNC80-deficient neurons.
temporal_context: The genetic defect is congenital and persistent in human UNC80 deficiency.
UNC80-null and severe C-terminal-truncation mouse phenotypes are evident neonatally, with apnea and death within the first postnatal day.
Extracellular-Ca2+ and neuropeptide effects are acute electrophysiological responses measured over seconds to minutes.
Developmental compensation and chronic circuit adaptation after UNC80 loss have not been separated from primary current loss.
profiles.uncertainty: The strongest disease-specific functional evidence is a reduced NALCN current from one human missense-variant equivalent in HEK293T cells and markedly reduced leak current in UNC80-null mouse hippocampal neurons. The focal state therefore has strong support as a UNC80-dependent electrophysiological mechanism, but transfer to the membrane potential and firing behavior of human patient neurons is an explicit inference. The direction should be described as reduced UNC80-dependent control, not as universal neuronal hypoexcitability, because spatial localization, residual variant function, neuronal conductance repertoire, acute modulators, developmental compensation, and circuit feedback can produce different net firing outcomes.
upstream_causes: Biallelic UNC80 loss-of-function or function-reducing variants
Reduced UNC80-dependent current potentiation despite retained NALCN and UNC79 binding in at least one missense variant
Loss of UNC79 recruitment and dendritic localization after disease-associated C-terminal UNC80 truncation
Reduced NALCN surface delivery and unresolved loss of channel-opening potentiation
Loss of extracellular-Ca2+ and neuropeptide/Src regulatory coupling

anatomical_context: C. elegans whole nervous system and whole-animal behavioral output
L4-to-adult lethargus-associated sleep circuitry
Stress-induced sleep circuitry after acute heat stress
Human central sleep-wake circuitry is clinically implicated only indirectly; no region-specific measurements exist for UNC80 deficiency.
profiles.causal_role: The focal abnormality is a downstream circuit-level consequence of unc-80 loss in the NCA channel complex and a proximal cause of abnormal sleep timing. Two unc-80 alleles and phenocopy by nca and unc-79 loss support a causal requirement for the complex; panneuronal nca-1 expression nearly completely restored developmentally timed sleep architecture in nca loss-of-function animals. The proposed transition from insufficient early sleep to delayed rebound is supported by experimental sleep deprivation but remains an inference rather than a direct measurement of homeostatic drive in unc-80 mutants.
cell_types: Neurons broadly: panneuronal nca-1 expression nearly completely rescued the developmentally timed sleep phenotype in nca loss-of-function animals.

Premotor interneurons and motor-neuron classes can support NCA-dependent arousal regulation in the earlier lethargus assay, but no single cell class was shown to mediate unc-80-dependent early fragmentation.
Human neural cell types responsible for sleep disturbance in UNC80 deficiency have not been identified.
contradictions: Huang et al. (2018) found normal total sleep and other L4-to-adult sleep measures in unc-80(e1272), whereas Kamijo et al. (2026), using different conditions and higher imaging frequency, found lower quiescence, fragmentation, prolonged sleep, and greater total quiescence. The later study offers a methodological explanation but does not fully resolve between-assay reproducibility.

During fragmented stress-induced sleep, unc-80 loss did not change the proportion responding to blue light, whereas the earlier developmentally timed sleep study found increased response latency during sleep bouts. The sleep paradigm, timing, and response metric differ, so the results constrain context rather than form a direct logical conflict.

nca loss and nca-1 gain of function can both reduce early quiescence, but only loss produces the prolonged rebound-like pattern; therefore channel direction alone does not predict the complete sleep phenotype.

In four reported people with biallelic UNC80 variants, two had sleep disturbance and two did not; one affected person had obstructive sleep apnea and another had difficulty initiating sleep. These clinical observations are heterogeneous and do not directly validate worm early-sleep fragmentation.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Early quiescence and quiescent-bout duration decrease while fragmentation increases.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: whole-animal C. elegans sleep circuitry during L4-to-adult transition and immediately after heat stress
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced early quiescent-bout stability
limitations: Behavioral quiescence is a whole-animal readout and does not identify the responsible neuronal subtype or electrical event.
The assays were conducted in liquid, although unchanged out-of-sleep quiescence argues against paralysis as the explanation.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Early developmentally timed and stress-induced sleep is consolidated into sustained quiescent bouts with relatively few transitions to motion.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: unc-80 loss shortens early quiescent bouts, prolongs motion bouts, lowers early quiescence, and increases transitions between quiescence and motion.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is the defining measured detail of the focal failure to stabilize early sleep.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Functional NCA-channel-complex contribution to sleep-state stabilization decreases.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans nervous system
distinct_mechanisms.label: Neuronal NCA-channel-complex dependence of sleep stabilization
limitations: Phenocopy supports a shared complex function but does not show that the three loss-of-function genotypes are mechanistically identical.
The neuronal rescue used nca-1 in nca loss-of-function animals rather than UNC80 rescue in unc-80 mutants.
The stress-induced-sleep rescue experiment was confounded by a channelrhodopsin transgene and did not establish a neuronal rescue for that context.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NCA-1/NCA-2, UNC-79, and UNC-80 jointly support neural regulation of stable developmentally timed and stress-induced sleep.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Loss of nca, unc-79, or unc-80 produces similar lower early quiescence and fragmented, prolonged sleep patterns; panneuronal nca-1 expression nearly completely restores the developmentally timed sleep phenotype of nca loss.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is the genetically supported upstream basis for the focal sleep-state instability, without establishing complex assembly, membrane voltage, or a specific circuit as the immediate mediator.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Measured noxious-stimulus responsiveness remains unchanged while sleep fragmentation increases.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: whole-animal C. elegans stress-induced sleep 30 minutes after heat stress
distinct_mechanisms.label: Fragmentation without reduced noxious-stimulus arousal threshold during stress-induced sleep
limitations: A single blue-light response assay may not capture arousal thresholds to other sensory modalities or at other times.
Response proportion is not identical to the latency measure used in the earlier developmentally timed sleep study.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Sleeping wild-type animals show a characteristic probability of responding to blue-light stimulation after heat stress.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Despite fragmented early stress-induced sleep, unc-80 loss-of-function animals had a response proportion to blue light that was not different from wild type.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This negative result constrains the focal mechanism by arguing against globally increased arousability as the cause of early fragmentation in this paradigm.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Delayed quiescence and sleep duration increase after insufficient early sleep.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans stress-induced and developmentally timed sleep
distinct_mechanisms.label: Rebound-like prolonged quiescence
limitations: The rebound interpretation is inferred from phenotypic similarity to experimentally sleep-deprived wild type; homeostatic drive was not directly measured in unc-80 mutants.
Delayed excess quiescence should not be conflated with the focal early fragmentation or with circadian locomotor output.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Adequate early stress-induced sleep is followed by declining quiescence over subsequent hours.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Reduced and fragmented early sleep is followed by elevated quiescence for 0.5-5 hours and prolonged sleep duration; early sleep deprivation in wild type reproduces this delayed pattern.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is a downstream compensatory pattern plausibly caused by the focal failure of early sleep stabilization.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Sleep-bout arousal threshold increases while waking sensory responsiveness is preserved.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans L4-to-adult developmentally timed sleep
distinct_mechanisms.label: Developmentally timed sleep-bout arousal-threshold elevation
limitations: The study reported normal sleep quantity and timing in unc-80 loss under its assay conditions, unlike the higher-frequency 2026 study.
The result is stimulus-, stage-, and metric-specific and does not establish a human arousal phenotype.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: During L4-to-adult sleep bouts, wild-type animals awaken to blue light with a characteristic response latency while remaining rapidly responsive during motion bouts.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: An earlier assay found increased blue-light response latency during sleep bouts in nca, unc-79, and unc-80 loss-of-function animals, with normal latency during motion bouts.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is a distinct NCA-complex-dependent sleep abnormality that may coexist with or vary independently from fragmentation; it is not part of the focal identity.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Deviation of NCA activity in either direction reduces early sleep consolidation, with genotype-specific downstream timing.
distinct_mechanisms.causal_level: ion-channel activity dependence of behavioral state
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans whole-animal sleep circuitry
distinct_mechanisms.label: NCA activity-range dependence of sleep architecture
limitations: Channel current or membrane voltage was not measured during these sleep assays.
The nca-1 gain-of-function phenotype is not equivalent to UNC80 deficiency and is included only to define the nonlinear biology of the same sleep-regulating complex.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NCA channel activity remains within a range compatible with timely entry into and maintenance of sleep bouts.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Both nca loss of function and nca-1 gain of function lowered developmentally timed sleep quiescence and produced fragmentation, but gain of function lacked the prolonged-duration and delayed-excess-quiescence pattern of loss of function.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This focal mechanistic detail shows that the unc-80-loss phenotype cannot be interpreted as a simple monotonic channel-activity-to-sleep-amount relationship.

downstream_consequences: Reduced early quiescence and shortened quiescent bouts
More frequent transitions between quiescence and motion
Prolonged developmentally timed and stress-induced sleep episodes
Delayed excess quiescence consistent with homeostatic rebound
Potential survival relevance after severe heat stress in nca mutants, although the unc-80 survival experiment was confounded and this consequence is not established for human disease.

established_pathology_observations.observation: unc-80(e1272) animals had lower average quiescence, shorter quiescent bouts, longer motion bouts, and more state transitions during L4-to-adult developmentally timed sleep than wild type.

During the first 30 minutes after heat stress, unc-80(e1272) animals showed reduced quiescence, shorter quiescent bouts, and more frequent quiescence-motion transitions, followed by elevated quiescence from 0.5 to 5 hours.
A second loss-of-function allele, unc-80(e1069), reproduced the developmentally timed and stress-induced sleep patterns of unc-80(e1272).

Wild-type animals deprived of the first 30 minutes of stress-induced sleep subsequently showed several hours of elevated quiescence resembling the delayed phase of the unc-80 loss-of-function pattern.
In an earlier L4-to-adult lethargus assay, unc-80(e1272) animals had normal total sleep and other sleep-quantity measures but increased response latency to blue light specifically during sleep bouts.

gaps: No polysomnography, actigraphy, bout-level sleep analysis, or arousal-threshold testing has established early sleep fragmentation in people with biallelic UNC80 variants.
No human UNC80-deficient neuron study has connected altered NALCN current, resting potential, or circuit activity directly to sleep-state instability.
The responsible C. elegans neuronal population and downstream circuit effectors for early fragmentation remain unresolved.
The relationship among NCA-complex function, EGL-4/PKG, and gap junctions is genetically supported for lethargus arousal but has not been shown to mediate the focal 2026 fragmentation phenotype.
The stress-induced-sleep neuronal rescue was technically confounded, so the cellular locus may differ between developmentally timed and stress-induced sleep.

The physiological importance of early sleep for survival is supported in nca loss- and gain-of-function mutants after severe stress, but the unc-80 survival result was confounded by a long-lived strain background.
It is unknown whether the worm rebound-like prolonged quiescence corresponds to any clinical sleep-wake-cycle reversal or other sleep phenotype in UNC80 deficiency.
mechanisms: Loss of unc-80 disrupts consolidation of the early sleep state, expressed as shortened quiescent bouts and more frequent transitions to motion.

Similar temporal phenotypes after nca, unc-79, or unc-80 loss and near-complete neuronal nca-1 rescue of developmentally timed sleep place sleep stabilization within neuronal NCA-channel-complex function.
Normal noxious-stimulus responsiveness during fragmented stress-induced sleep argues that this fragmentation is not explained by a globally lowered arousal threshold.
Insufficient early stress-induced sleep is followed by delayed excess quiescence resembling experimentally induced rebound sleep, consistent with preserved homeostatic compensation.

Both nca loss and nca-1 gain of function reduce early quiescence under some conditions, indicating that sleep architecture depends on an appropriate activity range rather than a monotonic relation to channel activity.
profiles.normal_state: During C. elegans L4-to-adult developmentally timed sleep and immediately after heat stress, quiescence rises promptly and is maintained in relatively consolidated bouts, with fewer transitions back to motion; baseline quiescence outside these sleep contexts is not elevated. Normal sleep architecture includes both appropriate state maintenance and context-appropriate arousability rather than a particular total sleep amount alone.
profiles.pathological_state: unc-80 loss of function reduces the early fraction of quiescence, shortens quiescent bouts, prolongs motion bouts, and increases quiescence-motion transitions. Developmentally timed sleep lasts longer and stress-induced sleep is followed by elevated quiescence for 0.5-5 hours, so total quiescence can increase despite poor early consolidation. The defect is therefore temporal instability of early sleep, not simply reduced total sleep.
profiles.summary: In two Caenorhabditis elegans unc-80 loss-of-function allele strains, developmentally timed sleep and the first 30 minutes of stress-induced sleep are unstable: early quiescence is reduced, quiescent bouts are shortened, motion bouts and state transitions increase, and the sleep episode is prolonged. Genetic phenocopy by nca and unc-79 loss and neuronal nca-1 rescue place the effect in NCA-channel-complex-dependent neural sleep regulation. Delayed excess quiescence is consistent with a homeostatic rebound from insufficient early sleep, but that causal interpretation is inferred from a matched wild-type sleep-deprivation experiment. Human UNC80-deficiency reports document heterogeneous sleep disturbance but do not establish this early-fragmentation mechanism in people.
temporal_context: Developmentally timed sleep during the C. elegans L4-to-adult transition
Early stress-induced sleep, especially 0-30 minutes after 37 degrees C heat stress
Delayed post-stress phase 0.5-5 hours after heat stress, when rebound-like quiescence appears
Baseline outside developmentally timed sleep and without heat stress, when unc-80 mutants did not show a general quiescence increase
Human reports span childhood but lack sleep-stage-resolved or longitudinal measurements.
profiles.uncertainty: Causality is strong for unc-80 loss producing the focal behavioral pattern in C. elegans because two alleles reproduce it, but molecular mediation is not measured and the human transfer is provisional. Developmentally timed sleep, stress-induced sleep, arousal threshold, circadian output, and clinical sleep-wake reversal are distinct biological variables. The profile preserves those distinctions: it treats the early fragmentation as focal, rebound-like prolonged quiescence as an indexed downstream process, and lethargus arousal-threshold elevation as an unindexed distinct finding. Human reports establish only that sleep disturbance can occur in UNC80 deficiency, not that it shares the worm mechanism.
upstream_causes: unc-80 loss of function in two C. elegans alleles
Loss of nca or unc-79, which phenocopies key temporal features and supports dependence on the NCA channel complex
Human biallelic UNC80 variants are the disease driver, but their causal connection to the specific early-fragmentation pattern remains untested.

anatomical_context: Developing brain after birth, inferred clinically from occipitofrontal circumference trajectories.
Cerebral hemispheres, where mild diffuse or regional atrophy is reported in a minority.
Corpus callosum, thin in one early cohort member but normal structural imaging predominated in that cohort.
profiles.causal_role: This profile is best treated as a variably expressed organ-growth phenotype downstream of biallelic UNC80 dysfunction, not as a proven primary cellular mechanism. Reduced postnatal brain growth could plausibly reduce neural tissue reserve during a period of rapid circuit maturation, but no study has shown that it independently causes the severe neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than marking the same underlying channelopathy, generalized growth failure, or secondary cerebral atrophy.
cell_types: No disease-specific cell type has been shown to drive the postnatal brain-growth phenotype.

Neurons are the best-supported cellular context for UNC80-NALCN channelosome function, but neuronal loss, impaired neurite growth, altered synaptogenesis, and glial contributions have not been tested against brain growth in affected individuals.
contradictions: Microcephaly is variably penetrant: the largest disease-specific cohort reported it in 7 of 10 evaluable individuals, not all affected individuals.
Structural MRI was normal in three of four individuals in one early cohort, and normal anatomy and myelination plus unrevealing postmortem neuroanatomy were reported in another family.

The large cohort described postnatal microcephaly but also stated that progressive microcephaly and cerebral atrophy had not been documented to the degree seen in PYCR2-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy.
Frequent co-occurrence of short stature and low BMI weakens a strictly brain-specific interpretation of reduced head growth.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Postnatal cranial and inferred brain growth are reduced relative to age-expected expansion.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: developing brain and cranial vault after birth
distinct_mechanisms.label: Decelerating postnatal head-growth trajectory
limitations: Available reports primarily use OFC rather than quantitative brain volume.
Individual longitudinal measurements are sparse and microcephaly is not universal.
OFC is an indirect proxy and cannot distinguish deficient tissue accrual from tissue loss or altered skull growth.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Occipitofrontal circumference and brain volume increase rapidly across infancy and continue increasing more slowly in the second postnatal year.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Head circumference shifts downward relative to age expectations after birth, sometimes reaching the microcephalic range in infancy or childhood.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is the longitudinal clinical detail that operationalizes the focal postnatal brain-growth-failure identity.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Cerebral tissue volume is reduced in a subset.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: cerebral hemispheres
distinct_mechanisms.label: Cerebral atrophy as a structural correlate in a subset
limitations: Atrophy is inconsistently present across UNC80 cohorts.
No serial volumetric imaging establishes onset, rate, or causal ordering relative to declining OFC.
One cohort explicitly noted that progressive microcephaly and cerebral atrophy were not documented to the degree seen in a differential diagnosis.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Cerebral tissue volume expands rapidly during infancy without diffuse volume loss.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Some affected individuals show mild diffuse or regional cerebral atrophy, whereas many others have structurally normal MRI.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Atrophy could contribute to reduced attained brain size or represent a downstream structural process, but single-time-point scans cannot establish whether it is the mechanism of postnatal growth failure.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Postnatal somatic growth and body mass are reduced alongside head-growth attainment.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: systemic growth and nutritional state
distinct_mechanisms.label: Concurrent generalized postnatal growth failure
limitations: The cohort data are cross-sectional and do not establish whether poor weight gain precedes head-growth deceleration.
No caloric, endocrine, metabolic, or body-composition study links generalized growth failure to the focal brain-growth phenotype.
The broad term failure to thrive does not identify a single biological mechanism.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Somatic linear growth, weight gain, and head growth proceed along age-appropriate trajectories with adequate nutritional status.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Short stature and low BMI frequently accompany postnatal microcephaly in UNC80 deficiency.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This parallel process may confound interpretation of a brain-specific growth defect and is a plausible contributor, but causation of reduced brain growth has not been tested.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: UNC80-dependent NALCN complex function and sodium-leak conductance are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: neuronal plasma membrane and NALCN channelosome
distinct_mechanisms.label: UNC80-dependent NALCN channelosome dysfunction
limitations: Functional current evidence is variant- and heterologous-cell-specific.
Effects on neural progenitor proliferation, survival, synaptogenesis, myelination, or tissue-volume accrual have not been measured in UNC80 deficiency.
The focal organ-growth phenotype cannot be causally assigned to this mechanism from current evidence.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC80 supports the neuronal NALCN-UNC79-UNC80 channel complex and its basal sodium-leak current.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Biallelic UNC80 loss-of-function or damaging variants impair channel-complex function and basal ionic conductance.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is an established upstream disease mechanism and a biologically plausible route to altered neurodevelopment, but no experiment links the channel defect specifically to reduced postnatal brain growth.

downstream_consequences: Acquired or postnatal microcephaly as the measurable clinical expression of reduced head-growth attainment.
Possible lower attained cerebral tissue volume or mild atrophy in a subset.
A possible contribution to severe neurodevelopmental impairment is biologically plausible but not separable from the direct functional effects of UNC80 channelopathy.

established_pathology_observations.observation: In four genetically defined affected individuals, birth OFC ranged from the 10th to 75th percentile where available, whereas later OFC ranged from 10th percentile to below the 3rd percentile, including one value of -4 SD.
In the 12-person IHPRF2 cohort, 7 of 10 evaluable individuals had postnatal microcephaly; postnatal short stature occurred in 6 of 9 and low BMI in all 8 evaluable individuals.

Neuroimaging in early UNC80 cohorts was frequently structurally normal: three of four individuals in one cohort had no structural anomaly, and a separately reported affected sibling had normal anatomy and myelination at 18 months; that sibling study also found no explanatory neuroanatomical abnormality on imaging or postmortem examination.

gaps: No published UNC80 cohort provides serial age-standardized MRI brain volumes spanning birth through early childhood.
No study distinguishes impaired tissue accrual from progressive tissue loss, altered skull growth, or secondary effects of systemic undernutrition.

No patient-derived neuronal, neural-progenitor, glial, organoid, or mammalian loss-of-function study measures proliferation, survival, neurite expansion, synaptogenesis, myelination, or regional brain volume as the mechanism of this phenotype.
Genotype, residual UNC80 function, nutritional status, seizure exposure, and respiratory illness have not been tested as modifiers of head-growth trajectory.
The relationship between head-growth trajectory and developmental outcome has not been quantified independently of overall disease severity.
mechanisms: Longitudinal deceleration of head-growth attainment after a birth OFC that may be within the reference range.
Possible reduction in cerebral tissue accrual or mild tissue-volume loss in the minority with atrophy, without serial volumetry to distinguish hypogrowth from atrophy.
Concurrent systemic growth failure and low BMI may contribute to or confound reduced cranial growth, but a nutritional or metabolic causal pathway has not been demonstrated.
profiles.normal_state: The healthy human brain undergoes rapid, regionally heterogeneous tissue-volume expansion after birth; quantitative MRI found total brain volume to increase about 101% in the first year and a further 15% in the second year, with most hemispheric expansion attributable to gray-matter growth.
profiles.pathological_state: In a subset of people with biallelic UNC80 variants, head circumference decelerates after birth or reaches the microcephalic range during infancy or childhood. Cohort evidence supports reduced postnatal head-growth attainment, but direct failure of brain-volume accrual has not been demonstrated by serial volumetric MRI and cannot yet be separated from generalized growth failure or occasional cerebral tissue loss.
profiles.summary: Biallelic UNC80 disease is associated in a subset of affected people with a postnatal fall in head-growth trajectory and later microcephaly despite birth measurements that can be within the reference range. This supports postnatal growth failure as a disease feature, but the organ-level formulation remains an inference: published cohorts generally report occipitofrontal circumference rather than serial quantitative brain volume, microcephaly is not universal, generalized short stature and low BMI commonly co-occur, and MRI ranges from normal to thin corpus callosum or mild cerebral atrophy.
temporal_context: Birth or early neonatal period can show a head circumference within or near the reference range.
Head-growth deceleration and microcephaly emerge postnatally across infancy or childhood in a subset.
The first two postnatal years are normally a period of especially rapid brain-volume expansion, making this the critical unresolved window for direct longitudinal measurement.
profiles.uncertainty: The focal identity is supported clinically as a postnatal growth-trajectory abnormality, but 'brain growth failure' is a treatment-blind mechanistic inference from OFC and occasional structural imaging rather than a directly measured cellular or volumetric process. Evidence is derived from small heterogeneous cohorts with incomplete longitudinal measurements; model, genotype, nutrition, and illness effects remain unresolved.
upstream_causes: Biallelic pathogenic UNC80 variants are the established genetic cause of the disorder.
UNC80-dependent NALCN channelosome dysfunction is an established disease mechanism but has not been connected experimentally to brain-tissue growth.
Concurrent severe feeding and systemic growth failure are plausible modifiers or confounders, not established causes of the focal phenotype.

anatomical_context: Distributed central neuronal networks, with generalized and multifocal EEG abnormalities rather than a consistently localized seizure focus.
Neuronal somata and dendrites within the NALCN-UNC79-UNC80 channelosome context.
Brain MRI may be normal in seizure-positive and seizure-negative individuals, so structural imaging does not define the focal abnormal state.
profiles.causal_role: Seizure is a downstream paroxysmal network manifestation rather than the primary molecular lesion. Biallelic UNC80 dysfunction is upstream, and impaired NALCN-channelosome conductance or localization provides a plausible excitability substrate; however, no experiment in patient-derived neurons has shown that either defect is sufficient for seizures, and severe UNC80 encephalopathy can remain non-epileptic.
cell_types: Central neurons; the disease-relevant human neuronal subtypes that initiate or propagate seizures are unresolved.
Cultured mouse hippocampal neurons in mechanistic knockout and localization experiments.
contradictions: Penetrance varies markedly: one aggregated series reported seizures in 13/34 individuals, while another six-person series was designed around severe non-epileptic encephalopathy and found only one isolated seizure episode without epileptiform EEG activity.
Severe developmental impairment and generalized EEG slowing can occur without seizures, so encephalopathy and epilepsy must not be treated as interchangeable outcomes.

Complete UNC80 loss reduces subthreshold inward sodium current and would be expected to hyperpolarize individual neurons, yet the clinical phenotype can include seizures; the compensatory, cell-type-selective, or circuit-level mechanism reconciling these directions is unknown.

Whole-cell NALCN current can be retained by a C-terminal truncation despite loss of dendritic localization, indicating that total current magnitude alone does not capture all disease-relevant channelosome dysfunction.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: NALCN-dependent subthreshold sodium conductance and UNC80-mediated resting-potential regulation are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: neuronal plasma membrane in cultured mouse hippocampal neurons
distinct_mechanisms.label: Loss of UNC80-dependent NALCN sodium-leak and resting-potential control
limitations: The causal electrophysiology was measured after complete Unc80 knockout in mouse neurons, not in neurons from people with biallelic UNC80 variants.

Reduced basal inward current may hyperpolarize individual neurons, whereas seizures are a network hyperexcitability phenotype; compensatory or cell-type-specific steps bridging those levels remain unknown.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC80 supports NALCN-mediated TTX-resistant subthreshold sodium leak current that contributes to neuronal resting-potential control.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: UNC80 loss markedly reduces NALCN-dependent sodium leak current in cultured hippocampal neurons.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Plausible upstream substrate for altered network excitability; linkage to seizure generation is inferred from the coexistence of channelosome dysfunction and human epilepsy, not directly demonstrated.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Dendritic UNC80 localization and spatial membrane-potential regulation are reduced while bulk somatic current can remain detectable.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: somata and dendrites of cultured mouse hippocampal neurons
distinct_mechanisms.label: Spatial loss of UNC80 from dendrites despite retained whole-cell current
limitations: The localization defect is variant-domain specific and cannot be generalized to every biallelic UNC80 genotype.
The study established localization and current phenotypes, not spontaneous seizures or epileptiform activity.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC80 reaches neuronal processes and supports spatial organization of the NALCN channelosome across somatic and dendritic compartments.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: C-terminally truncated UNC80 is retained in the soma and absent from neuronal processes despite retaining support for whole-cell NALCN current.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A mechanistically distinct upstream route that could alter dendritic integration and network stability; seizure causality was not tested.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Paroxysmal seizure activity and epileptiform network discharges are increased above normal absence.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: distributed central neuronal networks measured by scalp EEG
distinct_mechanisms.label: Mixed generalized and multifocal ictal expression
limitations: Seizure classification and EEG reporting were not standardized across the small retrospective case series.
The available records do not establish a single reproducible seizure syndrome or anatomical onset zone.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Neuronal networks do not generate recurrent generalized or multifocal paroxysmal seizure events or persistent epileptiform discharges.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Affected individuals can show generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, atonic, and atypical-absence seizures with spike-wave or multifocal EEG discharges.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is disease-specific semiologic and electrographic detail contained within the focal seizure identity.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Earlier seizure onset is associated with increased probability of refractory epilepsy.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: whole-patient longitudinal epilepsy phenotype
distinct_mechanisms.label: Early-onset refractory epilepsy trajectory
limitations: The analysis pooled 9 individuals with NALCN-related IHPRF1 and 8 with UNC80-related IHPRF2, so the association is not UNC80-specific.
The cross-sectional sample was small, and treatment histories and epilepsy ascertainment may influence the refractory classification.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: No recurrent seizures occur, so there is no age-of-onset or pharmacoresistant trajectory.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: In a pooled NALCN/UNC80 loss-of-function cohort, more than half of epilepsy was refractory and earlier onset was associated with refractoriness.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A downstream severity and temporal component of the focal seizure phenotype.

downstream_consequences: Recurrent generalized or multifocal clinical seizures and epileptiform EEG discharges in seizure-positive individuals.
A refractory epilepsy course in a subset; early onset may identify this trajectory, although current evidence is pooled across NALCN and UNC80 loss-of-function disorders.
Additional neurologic burden superimposed on severe developmental encephalopathy; the extent to which seizures independently worsen cognition is unresolved for UNC80 deficiency.

established_pathology_observations.observation: Four affected individuals from three families had seizures beginning between 3 months and 3 years 10 months; reported types included generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, atonic, and atypical-absence seizures, with encephalopathic EEG backgrounds and spike-wave or multifocal discharges.
In the 2018 aggregated UNC80 cohort, seizures were recorded in 1 of 12 newly described individuals and 12 of 22 previously published individuals, for 13 of 34 overall.

A separate six-person UNC80 series was predominantly seizure-negative: five had no seizures and one had a single episode without epileptiform discharges, demonstrating that profound congenital encephalopathy and nonspecific EEG slowing can occur without epilepsy.

In a 2025 cross-sectional channelosome cohort, the pooled loss-of-function group comprising IHPRF1 (NALCN) and IHPRF2 (UNC80) had frequent epilepsy; 58.8% of epilepsy was refractory, and earlier seizure onset was associated with refractoriness.
Cultured hippocampal neurons from UNC80-knockout mice had a drastic reduction in NALCN-dependent TTX-resistant sodium leak current; re-expression of UNC80 restored the current.

A disease-relevant C-terminal UNC80 truncation retained whole-cell NALCN current support but was retained in the soma and absent from neuronal processes, separating bulk current from spatial channelosome function.

gaps: No prospective UNC80-only natural-history cohort has standardized seizure semiology, serial EEG, age at onset, remission, and refractory status.
No patient-derived neuronal study directly links a biallelic UNC80 genotype, membrane-potential abnormality, and spontaneous epileptiform activity.
The neuronal populations and circuits responsible for seizure initiation in UNC80 deficiency are unknown.
UNC80-specific genotype-epilepsy correlations remain unresolved, including whether null, hypomorphic, and C-terminal trafficking-defective alleles carry different risks.
The degree to which seizures independently contribute to developmental severity, rather than covary with more severe channelosome dysfunction, is unresolved.
mechanisms: Reduced UNC80-dependent NALCN sodium leak conductance disrupts subthreshold membrane-potential regulation.
Variant-specific failure of UNC80 dendritic localization can disturb the spatial regulation of neuronal excitability even when whole-cell NALCN current is retained.
At the clinical network level, UNC80-associated seizures are heterogeneous in semiology and electrographic distribution, including generalized and multifocal patterns.
Earlier seizure onset marks a higher-risk refractory trajectory in a pooled NALCN/UNC80 loss-of-function cohort, but this has not been isolated statistically for UNC80 alone.
profiles.normal_state: Central neuronal networks maintain stable resting-potential and excitability control without spontaneous paroxysmal seizure events; subthreshold NALCN sodium conductance is distributed across neuronal somata and processes.
profiles.pathological_state: A subset of people with biallelic UNC80 variants develops recurrent paroxysmal seizures spanning generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, atonic, and atypical-absence phenotypes, often with encephalopathic, multifocal, or spike-wave EEG abnormalities. Onset and persistence vary substantially, and epilepsy is absent in many affected individuals.
profiles.summary: Seizure is a variably penetrant clinical neuronal-network phenotype in biallelic UNC80 disease. Disease-specific series document generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, atonic, and atypical-absence events with multifocal or spike-wave EEG abnormalities, but other molecularly confirmed individuals have severe congenital encephalopathy without epilepsy. Functional evidence supports an upstream channelosome model in which loss or spatial mislocalization of UNC80 impairs NALCN-dependent subthreshold sodium conductance and resting-potential control; the step from reduced single-neuron leak conductance to ictogenesis remains an inference rather than a directly demonstrated human mechanism.
temporal_context: Reported seizure onset in one deeply phenotyped four-person series ranged from 3 months to 3 years 10 months.
One individual in that series became seizure-free after age 3 years, whereas another required multiple ongoing antiseizure modalities, showing divergent persistence.
Earlier onset correlated with refractory epilepsy only in a pooled NALCN/UNC80 loss-of-function cohort.
Congenital encephalopathy precedes or occurs without epilepsy in many individuals, so seizure is not an invariant neonatal consequence.
profiles.uncertainty: The human evidence establishes seizure as a real but incompletely penetrant UNC80-deficiency phenotype, not a universal feature. The strongest quantitative refractoriness result pools NALCN- and UNC80-related loss-of-function disorders. The cellular evidence is causal for UNC80 control of NALCN current and localization in mouse neurons, but its connection to human ictogenesis is a cross-level inference. Variant, developmental-stage, neuronal-subtype, and circuit-specific effects could reverse or redistribute excitability in ways that bulk current measurements do not reveal.
upstream_causes: Biallelic pathogenic UNC80 variants, including truncating, splice-disrupting, and functionally abnormal missense alleles.
Loss of UNC80-dependent NALCN sodium-leak current and regulation of resting membrane potential.
For some C-terminal variants, somatic retention and loss of UNC80 from neuronal processes despite preserved bulk current.

anatomical_context: Generalized axial and appendicular neuromuscular system, with axial tone often prominently affected.
Central motor-control circuits, neuronal soma, axons, dendrites, presynaptic regions, and neuromuscular junctions are implicated by models.
Brain MRI may be normal or only mildly nonspecific, and one neurological autopsy did not reveal a structural lesion explaining the functional phenotype.
Skeletal muscle weakness or wasting occurs in some individuals, but no consistent primary muscle pathology has been established.
profiles.causal_role: Generalized hypotonia is a proximal functional manifestation of UNC80 deficiency and a major contributor to motor disability. The genetic association is strong and recurrent, and one patient variant directly reduces NALCN current. The proposed causal route is primarily central: loss of UNC80-dependent channelosome function reduces subthreshold excitability and sustained motor-network output, weakening tonic activation of the neuromuscular system. That localization remains an inference because human tone circuitry, motor neurons, peripheral nerves, neuromuscular junctions, and skeletal muscle have not been systematically interrogated.
cell_types: Human tone-regulating central neurons and spinal motor circuits are implicated clinically but have not been directly assayed.
Mouse hippocampal neurons were used to establish UNC80-dependent NALCN current and subcellular localization; they are mechanistic proxies rather than tone-specific neurons.
C. elegans HSN motor neurons showed preserved somatic but reduced synaptic calcium activity after unc-80 or NCA loss.
C. elegans premotor interneurons demonstrated NCA-dependent persistent activity that sustains locomotion.
Skeletal muscle fibers remain an incompletely evaluated downstream compartment; available biopsy evidence is nonspecific.
contradictions: Generalized hypotonia is not uniformly distributed: severe axial hypotonia can coexist with appendicular hypertonia or progressive spasticity.

Some affected individuals retain preserved deep-tendon reflexes and limited antigravity movement, arguing against complete failure of motor-neuron action-potential generation or a uniform peripheral neuropathy.
One cohort noted nonspecific myopathic biopsy changes, whereas other clinical reports and a neurological autopsy did not establish a primary structural muscle, nerve, spinal-cord, or brain lesion.

UNC80 C-terminal truncation can preserve whole-cell NALCN current while disrupting dendritic localization and UNC79 recruitment, showing that current amplitude alone does not capture all disease mechanisms.
The strongest activity-propagation and persistent-motor-circuit evidence comes from invertebrate NCA/unc-80 systems, and its transfer to human muscle tone is inferential.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Functional UNC80 dosage or activity is decreased.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: UNC80-expressing cells, with strongest functional evidence in nervous tissue
distinct_mechanisms.label: Loss of functional UNC80 from biallelic pathogenic variation
limitations: Not every reported variant has been tested for RNA or protein consequences.
Accessible patient fibroblasts may not express measurable UNC80, limiting direct human functional testing.
Variant-specific severity relationships remain uncertain.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Two functional UNC80 alleles provide sufficient neuronal UNC80 protein for channelosome regulation and localization.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Biallelic truncating, splice-disrupting, or functionally damaging missense variants markedly reduce effective UNC80 function.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Upstream disease driver recurrently associated with congenital or early persistent generalized hypotonia.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: NALCN channelosome stability, localization, and effective conductance are reduced in a variant-dependent manner.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: neuronal plasma membrane, soma, axons, and dendrites
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced stability and functional assembly of the NALCN channelosome
limitations: Direct current measurements are from heterologous cells and mouse neurons rather than patient-derived human neurons.
Different truncations separate whole-cell current from subcellular localization, so one uniform molecular defect cannot be assigned to all genotypes.
The quantitative contribution of channelosome impairment to muscle tone has not been measured.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC80 associates with NALCN and UNC79, supports channelosome assembly and localization, and potentiates NALCN current.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: UNC80 loss or disease-associated variants reduce NALCN current; some C-terminal truncations preserve somatic current yet lose UNC79 recruitment and neuritic localization.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Plausible molecular route between UNC80 deficiency and insufficient neural drive underlying generalized hypotonia.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: UNC80-dependent control of resting potential and basal neuronal excitability is reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: neuronal plasma membrane, including somatic and dendritic subthreshold compartments
distinct_mechanisms.label: Disturbed neuronal resting-membrane-potential and excitability control
limitations: Resting membrane potential has not been measured in neurons from people with biallelic UNC80 variants.
Most direct membrane-potential evidence concerns NALCN loss or model systems rather than the human hypotonia phenotype.
The relevant human neuronal populations for tone are not established.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NALCN-mediated background cation conductance contributes a depolarizing influence that positions neuronal resting potential for spontaneous and subthreshold activity.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Loss of UNC80-dependent NALCN current is inferred to reduce background inward conductance, hyperpolarize susceptible neurons, and lower basal or stimulus-coupled excitability.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: An upstream electrophysiological mechanism that could reduce tonic output from motor-control circuits and thereby lower whole-body tone.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Propagation or maintenance of excitation from neuronal soma and axon to synapse is reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans motor-neuron processes, presynaptic regions, and neuromuscular junctions
distinct_mechanisms.label: Failure of neuronal activity propagation to synaptic regions
limitations: This mechanism is demonstrated in C. elegans and has not been confirmed in human UNC80-deficient motor neurons or neuromuscular junctions.
The studied HSN egg-laying motor system is not anatomically homologous to human postural motor circuits.
Its quantitative contribution to generalized hypotonia is unknown.
