distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Depolarizing activity reaches presynaptic regions, evokes calcium transients, and supports transmitter release at neuromuscular synapses.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: In unc-80 or NCA-loss worms, somatic calcium dynamics can persist while synaptic calcium events, presynaptic activation, and neuromuscular transmission are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Provides a model-supported route by which active neurons may still deliver insufficient output to the neuromuscular apparatus, contributing to reduced tone.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Persistent motor-circuit activity and sustained locomotor output are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans premotor interneuron and neuromuscular locomotor circuit
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced persistent premotor-interneuron activity sustaining motor output
limitations: Evidence is from NCA loss in an invertebrate circuit, not from UNC80-deficient human or mammalian postural networks.
Locomotor persistence is not identical to resting muscle tone.
Translation to axial versus appendicular tone remains untested.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Premotor interneuron networks maintain persistent rhythmic activity after initiation, allowing motor programs and locomotion to continue.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: NCA loss weakens persistent premotor-network activity and produces frequent halting and reduced sustainability of locomotion.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A distinct circuit-level bridge from leak-channel dysfunction to inadequate sustained motor drive that could contribute to generalized low tone.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Muscle force and mass are reduced in at least a subset of affected individuals.
distinct_mechanisms.causal_level: whole-body neuromuscular performance and secondary tissue state
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: axial and appendicular skeletal muscle
distinct_mechanisms.label: Weakness and muscle wasting as potential amplifiers of low tone
limitations: Strength testing was limited by severe developmental impairment.
One reported muscle biopsy showed only nonspecific myopathic change.
No systematic electromyography, nerve conduction, neuromuscular-junction physiology, muscle imaging, or quantitative histopathology defines a peripheral mechanism.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Skeletal muscle mass and force are sufficient to express centrally generated postural tone and movement.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Several affected individuals had reduced strength, and some reports describe muscle wasting; prolonged immobility and undernutrition could further diminish the mechanical expression of tone.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: May amplify generalized hypotonia downstream of central dysfunction but is not established as its primary cause.

downstream_consequences: Severe delay or failure of head control, sitting, standing, and independent ambulation.
Reduced strength and possible secondary muscle wasting or deconditioning.
Possible contribution to impaired oral-motor coordination, feeding difficulty, and secretion clearance, although those are separate curated concepts and direct causal quantification is lacking.
Long-term immobility may contribute to contractures, scoliosis, and osteopenia, but these links are clinically plausible rather than established specifically for UNC80-related hypotonia.

established_pathology_observations.observation: Four genetically affected individuals had severe hypotonia beginning at birth or by three months and persistent hypotonia at last review from childhood through adolescence.
In one UNC80 cohort, all four individuals had major gross-motor impairment; none walked independently, and assessed strength was reduced in several individuals.
A person with biallelic UNC80 loss had severe truncal hypotonia from birth together with progressive peripheral spasticity, demonstrating regional and temporal mixture of low and high tone.

A disease-associated UNC80 p.Pro1700Ser-equivalent construct retained protein production and association with UNC79 and NALCN but produced significantly smaller NALCN currents than wild-type UNC80 in transfected HEK293T cells.

UNC80 knockout mice lacked brain UNC80 protein, had severely reduced neuronal NALCN current, apnea, and neonatal lethality; disease-analogous C-terminal truncation preserved whole-cell current but prevented normal neuritic localization and UNC79 recruitment.

In C. elegans, unc-80 or NCA loss reduced or silenced synaptic-region calcium transients despite preserved somatic calcium dynamics and reduced neuromuscular transmission with frequent locomotor halting.
C. elegans NCA loss impaired persistent rhythmic activity in a premotor interneuron network and reduced the sustainability of locomotion.

gaps: No study directly measures resting membrane potential, NALCN current, firing, or synaptic output in patient-derived UNC80-deficient motor neurons.
No quantitative clinical natural-history study separates axial from appendicular tone across age or distinguishes hypotonia from weakness, spasticity, dystonia, sedation, and deconditioning.
The relative contributions of brain, spinal interneurons, lower motor neurons, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction, and skeletal muscle are unresolved.
Systematic electromyography, nerve-conduction, repetitive-stimulation, muscle-imaging, and pathology data are lacking.
Variant-specific effects on channelosome assembly, current, trafficking, subcellular localization, and tone severity remain incomplete.
It is unknown which human motor-circuit cell types and developmental windows are most dependent on UNC80-NALCN function for normal tone.
mechanisms: Biallelic truncating or functionally damaging UNC80 variants reduce effective UNC80 activity in the nervous system.
Reduced UNC80 function impairs NALCN channelosome current, complex recruitment, cell-surface abundance, and variant-dependent neuritic localization.
Reduced NALCN-dependent background cation conductance is inferred to hyperpolarize relevant neurons or otherwise narrow their subthreshold excitability range.
UNC80/NCA loss in C. elegans preferentially weakens activity at axonal and synaptic regions, reducing neuromuscular transmission even when somatic calcium activity persists.
NALCN-family loss weakens persistent premotor-interneuron activity needed to sustain rhythmic movement, providing a model-level bridge from channel dysfunction to inadequate motor drive.
Clinical weakness, wasting, and immobility may amplify low tone, but evidence does not establish a primary myopathy or separate peripheral motor-neuron lesion.
profiles.normal_state: Normal whole-body tone requires continuous, appropriately scaled neural drive through central motor circuits, intact axonal and presynaptic signaling, effective neuromuscular transmission, and responsive skeletal muscle. Within the implicated pathway, functional UNC80 supports assembly, localization, and regulation of the UNC79-UNC80-NALCN channelosome; its background cation conductance helps place neuronal membrane potential in a range that permits basal and sustained circuit activity.
profiles.pathological_state: Affected individuals show globally reduced muscle tone, commonly evident at birth or in early infancy and persisting through childhood or adolescence. The low tone may be especially axial, can be accompanied by measurable weakness and muscle wasting, and drives severe delay or failure of sitting, standing, and independent ambulation. It may coexist with appendicular hypertonia or progressive spasticity, so the phenotype is not a uniform reduction of tone in every muscle group or at every age.
profiles.summary: Generalized hypotonia is a major, usually neonatal or early-infantile and persistent feature of biallelic UNC80 disease. Human series establish reduced tone across axial and appendicular systems, weakness, and profound gross-motor limitation, but do not directly localize the defect. Variant assays, UNC80-mutant mice, and invertebrate channelosome models support an inferred chain from impaired UNC80-dependent NALCN channelosome function to abnormal neuronal resting-potential control, weakened delivery of activity to synapses, and inadequate sustained motor-circuit output. This mechanistic chain is biologically coherent but has not been measured end-to-end in patient-derived motor neurons, spinal circuits, neuromuscular junctions, or muscle.
temporal_context: Onset is congenital, neonatal, or within the first months of life in reported cohorts.
Hypotonia commonly persists through childhood and has been documented into adolescence.
Tone distribution can evolve: persistent truncal hypotonia may coexist with or be followed by appendicular hypertonia and spasticity.
Secondary weakness, wasting, contracture, scoliosis, or deconditioning may become more influential with chronic immobility, but their individual trajectories are poorly quantified.
profiles.uncertainty: The phenotype itself is well established, but the mechanistic localization is provisional. Human genetic and clinical data support congenital persistent hypotonia downstream of biallelic UNC80 dysfunction; heterologous-cell and mouse-neuron data establish variant-dependent channelosome defects; worm studies supply causal evidence for synaptic propagation and persistent motor-network failure. No experiment yet links these levels in a human tone-specific system. Preserved reflexes, occasional nonspecific myopathic findings, normal or mild structural imaging, coexistence of spasticity, and variable residual motor ability leave central, peripheral, developmental, and secondary contributions only partly resolved.
upstream_causes: Biallelic UNC80 loss-of-function or functionally damaging variation.
Reduced effective UNC80 protein function, with variant-specific defects in NALCN current potentiation, UNC79 recruitment, surface expression, or neuritic localization.
Reduced or mislocalized NALCN channelosome conductance and impaired subthreshold excitability.
Reduced propagation of neuronal activity to presynaptic regions and weakened persistent motor-network output in model organisms.

anatomical_context: Diaphragm, intercostal, abdominal, and accessory respiratory musculature
Chest wall and intrathoracic conducting airways
Pharynx, larynx, and glottis
Central airways where mobilized secretions require cough-mediated extraction
Lower airways vulnerable to retained mucus, atelectasis, infection, and aspirated material
profiles.causal_role: Proximal organ-level respiratory-defense failure that can mediate between generalized hypotonia and retained airway secretions. Retained secretions can then increase susceptibility to mucus plugging, atelectasis, impaired gas exchange, and respiratory infection. This ordering is an inference from the focal human observation plus established neuromuscular cough physiology; it is not a measured causal pathway in UNC80-deficient respiratory muscles.
cell_types: Inspiratory and expiratory skeletal myofibers, implicated by general neuromuscular cough physiology but not directly assayed in UNC80 deficiency
Bulbar and laryngeal motor units controlling glottic closure, biologically relevant but unmeasured in the focal child
Airway ciliated epithelial cells and mucus-secretory cells, which participate in mucociliary clearance and infection-associated feedback; no intrinsic UNC80-related epithelial defect is established
contradictions: A 12-person biallelic UNC80 cohort recorded no breathing abnormalities (0/12), despite an increased tendency to infections in 8/12. This does not directly refute impaired cough because breathing-rhythm abnormalities and airway clearance are distinct, but it argues against treating the focal observation as a demonstrated cohort-wide respiratory phenotype.

Recurrent aspiration and aspiration pneumonia are independently documented in other UNC80 cases. These observations provide an alternative or coexisting route to pneumonia and cannot be collapsed into secretion-clearance failure.

The focal publication attributes clearance failure to hypotonia without objective respiratory physiology. The report therefore supports a clinical observation and author-assigned cause, not proof of the individual inspiratory, glottic, or expiratory mechanisms.
The reported child had 44 Mb homozygosity across 2q33.1-q37.3 plus smaller homozygous regions elsewhere, so additional recessive variation could modify the respiratory phenotype.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Respiratory and bulbar motor force or coordination is reduced
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: generalized axial, bulbar, inspiratory, and expiratory neuromuscular systems
distinct_mechanisms.label: Generalized hypotonia with respiratory-muscle involvement
limitations: Hypotonia is a clinical sign and does not by itself localize weakness to respiratory muscles.
No respiratory muscle strength, electromyography, spirometry, or cough-flow data were reported in the focal child.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Axial, inspiratory, expiratory, and bulbar neuromuscular systems provide sufficient tone, strength, and coordination for ventilation, airway protection, and cough.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Generalized hypotonia is present in UNC80 deficiency; in the focal child, the authors attributed inability to clear secretions to hypotonia, but did not identify or test specific respiratory-muscle groups.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Plausible upstream indexed phenotype that the focal case report explicitly names as the cause of secretion-clearance failure.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Expiratory pressure, peak cough flow, and proximal mucus movement are reduced
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: abdominal and expiratory respiratory muscles, intrathoracic central airways, and laryngeal outlet
distinct_mechanisms.label: Weak expiratory cough flow
limitations: Transfer from heterogeneous pediatric neuromuscular disorders to UNC80 deficiency is inferential.
The focal report contains no peak cough flow, maximal expiratory pressure, or cough-flow waveform.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Forceful expiratory contraction after glottic compression generates rapid outward airflow that transports central-airway secretions toward the larynx.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Neuromuscular weakness lowers expiratory pressure and flow, reducing proximal secretion transport and cough effectiveness.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Mechanistically informative focal detail that could explain the reported inability to clear secretions, although it was not directly measured in the UNC80 child.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Pre-cough lung inflation, tidal airway-caliber variation, and proximal mucus transport are reduced
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: diaphragm and inspiratory muscles, chest wall, and intrathoracic conducting airways
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced pre-cough inspiration and tidal mucus transport
limitations: No lung-volume, chest-wall, or inspiratory-pressure measurements were reported for the UNC80 child.
The child also used nocturnal BiPAP, so ventilatory impairment may coexist without proving this cough-phase defect.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Adequate inspiratory muscle activity produces a large pre-cough lung volume and normal tidal variation in airway diameter, supporting elastic recoil and proximal flow bias.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Inspiratory weakness can reduce pre-cough inflation and tidal volume, narrowing the mechanical reserve for cough and diminishing airway-diameter changes that normally assist mucociliary transport.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Mechanistically distinct focal detail within secretion-clearance failure; proposed from general neuromuscular physiology rather than demonstrated in the focal case.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Glottic closure, cough compression, and expulsive efficiency are reduced
distinct_mechanisms.causal_level: bulbar motor coordination and cough biomechanics
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: larynx, glottis, pharynx, and bulbar motor apparatus
distinct_mechanisms.label: Impaired glottic compression from bulbar dysfunction
limitations: No laryngoscopy, swallow study, cough-phase analysis, or bulbar respiratory examination was reported.
Oral-motor dysfunction and aspiration are related but separately curated pathologies and cannot be substituted for evidence of glottic cough failure.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Coordinated glottic closure during cough permits intrathoracic pressure accumulation before rapid glottic opening.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Bulbar or laryngeal weakness can compromise glottic closure and upper-airway coordination, limiting compressive pressure and the subsequent expulsive flow.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Potential focal detail that is biologically separable from inspiratory and expiratory muscle weakness; it remains unmeasured in the focal child.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Aspiration events and lower-airway foreign-material burden are increased
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: oropharyngeal-airway interface and lower respiratory tract
distinct_mechanisms.label: Recurrent aspiration as a parallel airway burden
limitations: The focal case report did not provide a swallow study or directly document aspiration in the reported child.
Aspiration observations from other UNC80 cases do not determine the cause of recurrent pneumonia in the focal child.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Swallowing and airway-protection reflexes prevent material from entering the lower respiratory tract.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Recurrent aspiration introduces oropharyngeal or gastric material into the airway and can independently promote pneumonia and add material that an already weak cough must clear.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Separate indexed sibling mechanism observed in other individuals with biallelic UNC80 variants; it can converge with secretion retention but does not establish the focal clearance defect.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Mucus load, retention, obstruction, and secondary clearance impairment increase
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: ciliated airway epithelium, mucus-producing cells, central and peripheral airways
distinct_mechanisms.label: Infection-amplified mucus-retention feedback
limitations: This feedback is established in general neuromuscular airway-clearance biology but was not measured longitudinally in UNC80 deficiency.
No sputum, microbiology, mucus-plug, atelectasis, bronchiectasis, or ciliary-function data were reported in the focal case.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Airway epithelium and cough remove baseline mucus and acute inflammatory secretions before they obstruct airways or sustain microbial growth.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: During infection, increased mucus production and ciliary injury add to a pre-existing weak cough; retained mucus then promotes plugging, atelectasis, recurrent infection, and further clearance impairment.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Downstream amplifier of the focal clearance failure and a plausible explanation for disproportionate morbidity during otherwise limited respiratory infections.

downstream_consequences: Retention of oral or airway secretions and reduced movement toward the larynx
Mucus plugging and microatelectasis
Impaired gas exchange and reduced respiratory reserve during acute illness
Increased susceptibility to recurrent lower respiratory infection and pneumonia
Potential infection-inflammation-ciliary injury feedback and, if persistent, chronic airway injury or bronchiectasis; these latter outcomes were not documented in the focal child

established_pathology_observations.observation: At age three years, the affected child used a cough-assist machine four times daily and was reported to be unable to clear secretions because of hypotonia.

The same child had reactive airway disease, recurrent pneumonia, nocturnal BiPAP use, and viral pneumonia during the reported admission; these establish respiratory morbidity but do not isolate which component resulted from impaired secretion clearance.

In a separate cohort of 12 individuals with biallelic UNC80 variants, 8 of 12 had an increased tendency to infections, while breathing abnormalities were recorded in 0 of 12; the cohort did not report cough-flow or secretion-clearance measurements.

gaps: No independent replication of chronic secretion-clearance failure in a genetically clean biallelic UNC80 cohort.
No peak cough flow, cough-flow waveform, maximal inspiratory or expiratory pressure, spirometry, lung volumes, or respiratory muscle imaging in the focal child.
No swallow study or laryngeal assessment to separate bulbar/glottic cough dysfunction from aspiration.
No data separating peripheral respiratory muscle weakness from central respiratory-drive abnormalities, restrictive chest-wall mechanics, or intrinsic lung disease.
No longitudinal natural history, age-specific incidence, genotype-phenotype correlation, or reproducible biomarker for the focal clearance phenotype.
No validated young-child threshold in the cited pediatric literature that can retrospectively classify this profoundly developmentally impaired three-year-old's cough effectiveness.
mechanisms: Reduced respiratory muscle force can limit the inspiratory volume available before cough and reduce normal tidal changes in airway diameter that aid proximal mucus movement.
Bulbar or laryngeal weakness can impair glottic closure during the compressive cough phase, limiting intrathoracic pressure generation.
Expiratory and abdominal muscle weakness can lower expiratory pressure and peak cough flow, decreasing movement of secretions toward the larynx.
Retained mucus can obstruct airways and foster atelectasis and infection; infection can add mucus and ciliary injury, forming a downstream positive-feedback loop.
Aspiration is a separate, independently observed UNC80-associated airway exposure mechanism that may coexist with clearance failure but must not be treated as evidence for the focal mechanism.
profiles.normal_state: Airway cilia and tidal-breathing flow bias move mucus proximally, while coordinated inspiratory, laryngeal/glottic, and expiratory muscle actions generate a high-flow cough that clears secretions from central airways by expectoration or swallowing.
profiles.pathological_state: In the focal child, secretion clearance was chronically insufficient and was explicitly attributed by the case authors to hypotonia. General pediatric neuromuscular physiology supports an inferred mechanism in which reduced inspiratory volume, impaired glottic compression, and/or weak expiratory flow diminish cough effectiveness and permit secretion retention, but none of these components was directly quantified in this patient.
profiles.summary: A single three-year-old child reported with UNC80-region homozygosity had chronic inability to clear respiratory secretions that the case authors attributed to hypotonia, requiring cough-assist use four times daily. Normal airway clearance couples mucociliary transport with an effective cough: sufficient inspiration expands the lungs, glottic closure permits pressure generation, and expiratory muscle contraction produces rapid flow that moves central-airway secretions toward the larynx for expectoration or swallowing. The disease-specific causal chain from generalized hypotonia to impaired cough mechanics is therefore biologically coherent, but the particular inspiratory, bulbar, and expiratory deficits were not measured in this child. Broader UNC80 cohorts establish frequent infection susceptibility but do not establish secretion-clearance failure as a general or primary feature. The focal mechanism is best retained as a case-level proximal respiratory vulnerability, distinct from aspiration, central ventilatory control, intrinsic immune dysfunction, and infection itself.
temporal_context: The direct observation was chronic at age three years, with scheduled cough-assist use four times daily rather than only during the reported acute illness.
Acute viral respiratory infection can increase secretion load and further reduce respiratory reserve, making a baseline clearance deficit clinically more consequential.
The onset, progression, and stability of impaired clearance across infancy, childhood, and different UNC80 genotypes are unknown.
profiles.uncertainty: Direct disease-specific evidence is limited to one descriptive case, and that child's broad homozygous genomic regions complicate attribution to UNC80 alone. The detailed cough-phase mechanisms are biologically grounded in pediatric neuromuscular literature but remain transfer inferences, not measurements in UNC80-deficient muscle, motor neurons, or airway tissue. Infection, aspiration, central ventilatory abnormalities, feeding dysfunction, chest-wall mechanics, and intrinsic pulmonary disease may coexist and were not partitioned. Frequent infections in a broader UNC80 cohort support respiratory vulnerability but do not identify impaired secretion clearance as the cause.
upstream_causes: Generalized hypotonia was the cause assigned by the focal case authors, but the specific respiratory, bulbar, central, or peripheral neuromuscular lesion was not localized.
Reduced inspiratory muscle force, impaired glottic closure, and reduced expiratory muscle force are plausible intermediate causes inferred from pediatric neuromuscular cough physiology.
The focal child's broad regions of homozygosity make attribution to UNC80 alone less secure than in a case with isolated biallelic UNC80 variants.

anatomical_context: C. elegans nerve ring
C. elegans ventral and dorsal nerve cords
predominantly nonsynaptic regions along neuronal processes
neuronal somata, axons, dendrites, and synaptic regions as experimentally distinguished compartments
mammalian cell plasma membrane in reconstitution assays
profiles.causal_role: UNC-80 is causally required for normal axonal localization of the NCA pore-forming channel orthologue in the worm: loss of unc-80 removes the axonal NCA-1 signal and gene-specific re-expression restores it. The study's combined localization, calcium-imaging, and genetic data place channel-localization failure upstream of reduced excitation at synaptic regions, but the causal chain from localization to propagation is a supported model rather than a direct isolation of localization from every other UNC-80 function. Transfer to human UNC80 deficiency is mechanistic inference from conserved channel-complex biology.
cell_types: C. elegans neurons broadly expressing unc-80 and nca-1
C. elegans nerve-cord motor neurons
C. elegans HSN egg-laying motor neurons
C. elegans premotor interneurons in the NLF-1/NCA functional study
cultured mouse hippocampal neurons in the UNC80 truncation localization study
heterologous mammalian cells reconstituting the NALCN-FAM155A-UNC79-UNC80 complex
contradictions: The two independent worm studies agree that UNC-80 is required for proper NCA-channel localization; no direct contradictory C. elegans localization result was found.

A mammalian UNC80 C-terminal truncation caused somatic retention and loss from axons and dendrites yet still supported robust whole-cell NALCN current, demonstrating that whole-cell current and neurite localization can be experimentally dissociated.

The focal source describes UNC-80 as necessary and sufficient to restore NCA-1 axonal localization in the transgenic worm assay, but does not show that UNC80 alone is sufficient for channel localization outside the intact NCA/UNC79/NLF-1 machinery.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Axonal NCA-channel localization is reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans nerve-ring and nerve-cord axons
distinct_mechanisms.label: UNC80-dependent axonal localization of NCA pore-forming subunits
limitations: Directly demonstrated in C. elegans rather than human neurons.
The staining assays do not distinguish failed translation, transport, membrane insertion, clustering, or local protein stability.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NCA-1 and NCA-2 proteins occupy neuronal processes, with NCA-1 enriched at punctate nonsynaptic axonal regions of the nerve ring and nerve cords.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: unc-80 loss eliminates or markedly reduces axonal NCA-1 staining and prevents proper localization of NCA-1/NCA-2 channel subunits.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is the core experimentally observed identity of the focal profile.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: The ratio of localized axonal NCA-1 protein to nca-1 transcript is reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans neurons and their axonal processes
distinct_mechanisms.label: Post-transcriptional loss of axonal NCA-1 protein
limitations: Transcript was measured in mixed-stage whole animals, whereas protein localization was assessed in neuronal processes.
Translation, trafficking, clustering, and stabilization were not experimentally separated.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Normal nca-1 transcript is accompanied by detectable axonal NCA-1 protein.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: nca-1 transcript remains near wild-type abundance in unc-80 mutants while axonal NCA-1 staining disappears or is markedly reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This narrows the focal localization failure to a post-transcriptional step but does not identify which protein-handling step fails.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: ER-to-axon delivery of NCA channel and associated sodium leak are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans neuronal endoplasmic reticulum, axons, and premotor interneurons
distinct_mechanisms.label: NLF-1-dependent ER delivery of NCA channels to axons
limitations: The perturbation is nlf-1 loss rather than unc-80 loss.
It provides pathway context and cannot be assigned as the molecular cause of the focal UNC80-dependent defect.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: The ER-resident factor NLF-1 promotes axonal localization of NCA reporters and supports NCA-dependent sodium leak.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: nlf-1 loss reduces axonal NCA localization, sodium leak current, and premotor-interneuron excitability.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is an independently demonstrated upstream delivery mechanism capable of producing a similar localization defect, but no evidence shows that NLF-1 is abnormal in UNC80 deficiency.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: NALCN plasma-membrane localization is reduced when channel-complex interactions are disrupted.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: heterologous mammalian-cell plasma membrane
distinct_mechanisms.label: UNC79-UNC80 interaction-dependent NALCN surface localization
limitations: The assay used overexpressed mammalian channel components in heterologous cells.
Cell-surface abundance does not resolve axonal versus somatic localization.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: The UNC79-UNC80 heterodimer binds cytoplasmic regions of NALCN and strongly promotes NALCN cell-surface localization in the reconstituted mammalian channel complex.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Disruption of NALCN interaction motifs for the UNC79-UNC80 heterodimer reduces NALCN surface localization and current.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This is a conserved mammalian mechanistic analogue of the focal channel-localization dependency, not direct evidence of axonal localization in UNC80-deficient human neurons.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: NALCN-complex stability and functional assembly are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: NALCN-UNC79-UNC80 complex at neuronal membranes
distinct_mechanisms.label: NALCN channel-complex destabilization
limitations: The focal worm experiments do not quantify assembled complex abundance separately from subcellular localization.
The relative contribution of degradation versus mislocalization remains unresolved.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NALCN or NCA pore-forming proteins and UNC79-UNC80 auxiliary proteins are mutually supported within a stable, localized channel complex.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Loss of one complex component reduces the localization or abundance of other components, so complex destabilization can accompany channel-localization failure.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This indexed sibling is a plausible upstream or concurrent process but is broader than the focal axonal channel-localization state and is not duplicated as a new node here.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Propagation of excitation from neuronal somata to synaptic regions is reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans HSN neuronal cell bodies, axons, and synaptic regions
distinct_mechanisms.label: Failure of neuronal activity propagation to synapses
limitations: The ordering from axonal NCA-1 loss to failed synaptic propagation is a synthesis across experiments rather than a localization-selective intervention.
Human neuronal transfer is untested.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Rhythmic neuronal activity detected in the cell body is conveyed to synaptic regions, where calcium transients support synaptic output.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: In unc-80 mutants, somatic rhythmic calcium events persist while synaptic-region calcium transients are less frequent or silenced in a subset of animals.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This indexed downstream electrophysiological process was observed in the same model and is mechanistically connected by the paper's channel-localization and propagation model, but localization was not selectively manipulated independently of other UNC-80 functions.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: NCA-dependent sodium leak and neuronal excitability are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans premotor interneurons
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced NCA-dependent sodium leak and excitability
limitations: The direct delivery-to-current experiment perturbed nlf-1 or nca, not unc-80.
Resting membrane potential and NALCN current have not been directly measured in patient-derived UNC80-deficient neurons.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Axonally delivered NCA channel contributes sodium leak that supports resting membrane potential and premotor-interneuron excitability.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Loss of NCA or its localization factor NLF-1 reduces sodium leak current, hyperpolarizes resting membrane potential, and lowers premotor-interneuron activity.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: This indexed electrophysiological process is a functional consequence of deficient channel delivery in the nlf-1 model and is consistent with the focal state, but was not directly measured as a consequence of UNC80 loss in human neurons.

downstream_consequences: Reduced frequency or silencing of calcium transients at synaptic regions despite persistence of somatic transients in a subset of unc-80 mutant animals.
Reduced synaptic transmission and fainter locomotor behavior in the broader NCA/UNC-80 loss-of-function model.

Reduced sodium leak current, hyperpolarized resting membrane potential, and decreased premotor-interneuron activity when NCA delivery is disrupted by nlf-1 loss; this supplies pathway-level consequence evidence but is not a direct UNC80-deficient human measurement.

established_pathology_observations.observation: NCA-1 staining was eliminated or greatly reduced in the nerve ring and nerve cords across multiple unc-80 mutant alleles.
An UNC-80::RFP transgene restored punctate NCA-1 staining in the nerve ring and along nerve cords of unc-80 mutants.
nca-1 transcript abundance remained approximately wild type in unc-80 mutants even when axonal NCA-1 protein staining was lost.
Co-expression of mammalian UNC79 and UNC80 promoted NALCN cell-surface localization in a heterologous expression system.

gaps: No study directly demonstrates reduced axonal NALCN localization in neurons from a person with biallelic UNC80 variants.
The exact post-transcriptional defect in unc-80 mutants—translation, ER exit, axonal transport, membrane insertion, clustering, or local stabilization—remains unresolved.
No quantitative relationship has been established between residual UNC80 expression or variant class and axonal NALCN abundance.
The developmental timing, cell-type distribution, and reversibility of channel-localization failure in human neurons are unknown.
Somatic whole-cell NALCN current may remain robust despite neurite-localization failure, so compartment-resolved electrophysiology is needed to connect localization with human neuronal function.
mechanisms: Post-transcriptional dependence of axonal NCA-1 protein localization on UNC-80, with retained nca-1 transcript excluding transcriptional loss as the primary explanation.

Reciprocal localization dependence among NCA-1, UNC-80, and UNC-79, consistent with channel-complex assembly, transport, anchoring, clustering, or stabilization along nonsynaptic axonal membrane regions.

A separate ER-resident localization factor, NLF-1, promotes NCA axon delivery; NLF-1 loss reduces NCA-dependent sodium leak, linking delivery of the channel to electrical function without establishing that NLF-1 is altered in UNC80 deficiency.

In mammalian heterologous cells, physical association of the UNC79-UNC80 heterodimer with NALCN promotes channel cell-surface localization; disrupting two interaction motifs lowers surface localization and whole-cell current.

UNC80 neurite localization can be dissociated from robust whole-cell NALCN current in cultured mammalian neurons, showing that somatic whole-cell current does not by itself demonstrate correct axonal or dendritic channel-complex distribution.
profiles.normal_state: NCA-1 is enriched in punctate, predominantly nonsynaptic regions of C. elegans axons in the nerve ring and nerve cords, alongside axonally localized UNC-80 and UNC-79; normal nca-1 transcription is accompanied by channel protein localization. In mammalian experimental systems, UNC79 and UNC80 associate with NALCN and promote its cell-surface localization, while full-length UNC80 reaches neuronal processes.
profiles.pathological_state: Across multiple C. elegans unc-80 loss-of-function alleles, NCA-1 axonal staining is eliminated or greatly reduced despite retained nca-1 transcript, indicating a post-transcriptional localization defect. The exact failed step among translation, trafficking, membrane delivery, clustering, and local stabilization was not resolved in the focal worm experiment.
profiles.summary: In Caenorhabditis elegans, UNC-80 loss leaves nca-1 transcript detectable at approximately wild-type abundance but eliminates or markedly reduces NCA-1 protein staining in the nerve ring and nerve cords; re-expression of UNC-80 restores axonal staining. Independent worm work likewise identifies UNC-80 as required for NCA-1/NCA-2 localization. Mammalian cell and neuronal studies support conservation of an UNC79-UNC80-dependent channel-surface or neurite-localization function, but they do not establish that people with biallelic UNC80 variants have the same axonal pore-subunit defect.
temporal_context: Mixed-stage C. elegans were used for transcript analysis.
The focal localization phenotype was assessed in established loss-of-function mutant animals; developmental onset and reversibility were not temporally resolved.
Mammalian localization experiments used transiently transfected cultured cells or neurons and do not establish developmental timing in UNC80 deficiency.
profiles.uncertainty: The focal abnormal state is causal and reproducible in C. elegans unc-80 loss-of-function models and is independently supported by two worm studies. Mammalian data establish conserved UNC79-UNC80 roles in NALCN surface localization and UNC80 neurite trafficking, but no human UNC80-deficient neuron has been shown to lose axonal NALCN. It is therefore uncertain whether the human disease lesion is a quantitatively similar pore-subunit localization failure, which neuronal compartments are most affected, and whether loss of channel localization or another UNC80-dependent complex function dominates pathogenesis.
upstream_causes: C. elegans unc-80 loss-of-function alleles directly cause the focal loss of NCA-1 axonal staining.
Loss of UNC79 also reduces or eliminates axonal NCA-1 and UNC-80 localization, demonstrating reciprocal dependence among channel-complex components.
Loss of NLF-1 independently reduces axonal delivery of NCA reporters, defining a parallel or upstream trafficking dependency rather than an established lesion in UNC80 deficiency.
Disrupted UNC79-UNC80 binding to NALCN reduces mammalian channel cell-surface localization in reconstitution assays.

anatomical_context: HSN neuronal cell bodies and their presynaptic regions on vulval muscles
Nonsynaptic axonal regions of the nerve ring and ventral/dorsal nerve cords
Cholinergic and GABAergic neuromuscular junctions used to measure downstream synaptic output
profiles.causal_role: The unc-80 loss-of-function genotype causally produces a compartment-selective failure of presynaptic activation in the worm HSN circuit and phenocopies NCA-channel loss. The evidence supports UNC-80 as necessary for NCA-dependent propagation of excitation along neurites, while the specific electrical intermediate is inferred because membrane voltage was not recorded continuously along the axon.
cell_types: Serotonergic HSN motor neurons, in which soma and presynaptic calcium were imaged simultaneously
GABAergic and cholinergic motor neurons contributing to independently measured neuromuscular-junction transmission
UNC-80-expressing command interneurons AVA and AVE and guidepost neuron AVG, providing independent circuit-localization context but not a direct test of HSN propagation
contradictions: The remaining synaptic calcium-transient trains in unc-80 mutants retain approximately normal amplitude and temporal coupling to somatic trains; the defect is therefore probabilistic silencing or failed initiation rather than uniform attenuation of every transmitted event.
Normal-appearing HSN somatic calcium dynamics argue for a spatial propagation defect, but the constitutively activating assay could mask an additional defect in neuronal firing.
Reduced synaptic transmission is compatible with propagation failure but is not specific to it; altered firing or vesicle release were not excluded.

Loss of unc-7 restores evoked postsynaptic-current amplitude in an nca-loss background while leaving resting spontaneous event frequency reduced, showing that basal and strongly evoked output can dissociate.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Functional NCA-channel-complex assembly and stability are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: neuronal NCA-1/NCA-2-UNC-79-UNC-80 channel complex
distinct_mechanisms.label: UNC-80-dependent NCA-channel-complex stability and function
limitations: The focal worm study establishes functional interdependence and localization effects but does not directly quantify complex stoichiometry, lifetime, or biochemical stability.
Human variant-specific effects on complex assembly may differ from null-allele effects in worms.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC-80 participates with UNC-79 and the NCA pore-forming subunits in a functional neuronal channel complex.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Loss of unc-80 produces NCA-loss-like physiological and behavioral phenotypes, consistent with reduced functional NCA-complex availability.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Upstream prerequisite for the axonal channel activity that supports soma-to-synapse propagation.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Axonal NCA-channel localization is reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans nerve-ring and nerve-cord axons
distinct_mechanisms.label: UNC-80-dependent axonal NCA-1 localization
limitations: Localization and propagation were measured in separate assays; the localization defect was not quantitatively linked animal-by-animal to synaptic silencing.
Conservation of this subcellular phenotype in human UNC80-deficient neurons has not been demonstrated.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NCA-1 is present along nerve-ring and nerve-cord axons, enriched at nonsynaptic neuritic regions where it can support propagation.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: NCA-1 staining is eliminated or greatly reduced across multiple unc-80 alleles, reducing axonal availability of the channel.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Upstream localization defect that provides a spatially coherent explanation for preserved somatic activity but failed presynaptic activation.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: UNC-80-dependent control of neuronal membrane potential and excitability is reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: neuronal plasma membrane along axonal processes
distinct_mechanisms.label: Loss of neuritic membrane-excitability support
limitations: The HSN experiment used calcium imaging rather than direct axonal voltage recording.
The resting-potential role is established for mammalian NALCN, but direct transfer to UNC80-deficient human neurons remains provisional.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NCA-channel conductance helps maintain neuritic membrane excitability so depolarizing signals can reach presynaptic regions.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: UNC-80/NCA dysfunction lowers the probability that somatic activity produces presynaptic activation, consistent with insufficient depolarization along the neurite.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Electrophysiological intermediate proposed between channel-complex dysfunction and the focal spatial propagation failure.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: The probability and frequency of presynaptic calcium-transient initiation are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: serotonergic HSN presynaptic regions in adult C. elegans
distinct_mechanisms.label: Failure to initiate presynaptic calcium transients
limitations: Calcium transients are a proxy for electrical arrival and local channel activation, not a direct measurement of propagated voltage.
The assay constitutively activated HSN neurons and may have masked an additional somatic firing defect.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Somatic calcium-spike trains are accompanied by temporally coupled calcium transients in HSN presynaptic regions.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Presynaptic calcium-transient trains are absent in about half of unc-80 mutants and reduced in frequency across the group despite persistent somatic trains.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Directly measured focal detail that operationalizes the soma-to-synapse propagation failure.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Spontaneous and evoked synaptic output are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans cholinergic and GABAergic neuromuscular junctions
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced synaptic transmission downstream of NCA dysfunction
limitations: The independent electrophysiology used nca loss rather than unc-80 loss, so equivalence depends on the demonstrated functional interdependence of the complex.
The transmission deficit cannot be assigned exclusively to propagation because firing and vesicle-release defects were not excluded.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NCA-dependent neuronal excitation supports normal spontaneous event frequency and robust electrically evoked postsynaptic currents at neuromuscular junctions.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: NCA loss lowers spontaneous postsynaptic-current frequency and markedly reduces electrically evoked postsynaptic-current amplitude.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A downstream functional consequence consistent with failures of excitation reaching presynaptic sites, although release machinery and firing defects may also contribute.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Loss of UNC-7 selectively increases evoked synaptic output in the NCA-loss background without normalizing resting spontaneous event frequency.
distinct_mechanisms.causal_level: ion-channel interaction and state-dependent neuronal excitability
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: C. elegans neurons controlling neuromuscular-junction output
distinct_mechanisms.label: State-dependent antagonistic modulation by UNC-7 innexin
limitations: This interaction was tested in nca loss, not directly in unc-80 mutants.
The physical or biophysical basis is unresolved, and the authors found no obvious NCA-1/UNC-7 colocalization.
Restored evoked postsynaptic current does not show that soma-to-synapse propagation or human UNC80 pathology is restored.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: UNC-7 and NCA activities jointly shape neuronal output, with NCA dominating basal neuromuscular-junction activity and UNC-7 exerting an opposing influence after strong stimulation.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: In nca loss-of-function animals, spontaneous event frequency remains low, but removing unc-7 restores electrically evoked postsynaptic-current amplitude toward wild type.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: An independently observed modifier of downstream NCA-dependent synaptic output; it does not establish correction of the focal HSN propagation defect.

downstream_consequences: Intermittent or absent activation of presynaptic calcium transients despite ongoing somatic rhythms
Reduced spontaneous postsynaptic-current frequency and reduced electrically evoked synaptic output in NCA-loss models
Failure to sustain normal locomotor activity and circuit-specific behavioral responses in unc-80/NCA-pathway mutants
Potentially unreliable activation of synaptic targets, inferred from the presynaptic and postsynaptic measurements

established_pathology_observations.observation: In unc-80 mutant adults, HSN cell-body calcium-transient frequency was 5.1 +/- 1.3 spikes/min and not significantly different from wild type, whereas half of animals had silent synaptic regions and aggregate synaptic frequency fell to 0.9 +/- 0.7 spikes/min, lower than both unc-80 cell bodies and wild-type synapses.

NCA-1/NCA-2 loss produced the same compartment-selective pattern: preserved HSN somatic calcium dynamics with absent synaptic transients in half of animals and reduced synaptic transient frequency overall.

In an independent C. elegans study, nca loss reduced electrically evoked neuromuscular-junction postsynaptic-current amplitude by approximately 60 percent, independently corroborating impaired evoked synaptic output downstream of NCA-complex dysfunction.

gaps: No human UNC80-deficient neuron study directly measures axonal voltage propagation, presynaptic calcium activation, or synaptic transmission.
Direct voltage imaging or electrophysiology along the soma-axon-synapse axis is needed to distinguish propagation failure from changes in firing and local presynaptic excitability.
The focal calcium phenotype has not been mapped across neuronal classes, developmental stages, or specific human disease alleles.
It is unknown whether restoring UNC-80 after circuit development normalizes the propagation phenotype or whether developmental abnormalities make it persistent.
The mechanistic basis of the UNC-7/NCA interaction and its relevance to UNC80 loss rather than NCA loss remain unresolved.
mechanisms: UNC-80-dependent assembly and function of the NCA-1/NCA-2 channel system
UNC-80-dependent axonal localization of NCA-1
maintenance of neuritic membrane excitability sufficient to convey depolarizing activity
initiation of calcium transients at presynaptic regions after somatic activity
preservation of spontaneous and evoked synaptic output
state-dependent antagonistic modulation of NCA-dependent synaptic output by UNC-7 innexin
profiles.normal_state: UNC-80 supports the axonal NCA-1/NCA-2 channel system so that depolarizing activity arising in the neuronal cell body is maintained along neurites and can initiate temporally coupled calcium transients at presynaptic regions, enabling normal synaptic output.
profiles.pathological_state: With unc-80 loss of function, HSN cell bodies retain rhythmic calcium transients, but presynaptic regions frequently become silent and show a lower mean transient frequency. The spatial dissociation indicates loss of reliable soma-to-synapse activity propagation rather than loss of all somatic rhythmic activity.
profiles.summary: In adult C. elegans, UNC-80 is required for an NCA-channel-dependent spatial coupling between rhythmic activity in a neuronal soma and activation at its presynaptic region. In unc-80 loss-of-function animals, serotonergic HSN somatic calcium-spike dynamics remain detectable while synaptic-region transients are absent in about half of animals and reduced in aggregate, supporting a selective failure to convey depolarizing activity to synapses. This is causal animal-model pathology, but transfer to human UNC80-deficient neurons is untested.
temporal_context: The focal calcium-imaging assay used adult C. elegans 24 hours after the L4 stage.
Recordings were made during a 10-minute immobilized assay under conditions that stimulate constitutive HSN activation.
The evidence addresses mature circuit function rather than developmental acquisition or progressive degeneration of propagation capacity.
profiles.uncertainty: The focal result is strong, causal, compartment-resolved evidence in an invertebrate unc-80 loss-of-function model, not a direct observation in human disease. The designation 'propagation failure' is a synthesis from preserved somatic calcium rhythms, reduced presynaptic transients, nonsynaptic axonal NCA localization, and reduced downstream synaptic output. Because axonal voltage was not recorded and the assay constitutively activated HSNs, contributions from altered firing, local calcium-channel recruitment, or vesicle release cannot be fully separated. Independent work localizes UNC-80 function to defined worm interneurons and corroborates NCA-dependent synaptic-output defects, but does not independently reproduce the HSN soma-to-synapse calcium phenotype.
upstream_causes: unc-80 loss-of-function alleles
Reduced functional assembly and stability of the UNC-79/UNC-80/NCA channel complex
Loss or marked reduction of axonal NCA-1 localization
Reduced NCA-dependent neuritic membrane-excitability support

anatomical_context: Stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract in one three-year-old child with a clinical UNC80-disease label.
Cultured neonatal mouse small-intestinal interstitial cells of Cajal for the NALCN pacemaker-modulation evidence.
Colon and distal bowel for the independently observed severe constipation and CT stool burden; this is a separate segment from the focal gastric process.
profiles.causal_role: At present, delayed gastric emptying is best placed as a possible organ-level expression of generalized neuromuscular dysfunction in UNC80 deficiency and as one contributor to feeding intolerance, vomiting vulnerability, and poor growth. The direct human evidence does not establish whether the proximal defect is vagal/enteric-neuronal signalling, interstitial-cell-of-Cajal modulation, gastric smooth-muscle contractility, pyloric coordination, secondary effects of severe hypotonia and immobility, or non-disease factors. The proposed UNC80-to-NALCN-to-ICC-to-slow-transit chain is an inference assembled from separate human heterologous-cell and mouse intestinal-cell experiments, not a demonstrated causal pathway in UNC80-deficient gastric tissue.
cell_types: Interstitial cells of Cajal: directly studied only in cultured neonatal mouse small intestine; relevance to human UNC80-deficient stomach is inferred.
Gastrointestinal smooth-muscle cells: physiologically coupled to ICC slow waves but not directly assayed in UNC80 deficiency.
Enteric neurons and autonomic inputs: plausible sources of substance P and coordinated motility signals, but not directly assayed in the focal child.
Skeletal and respiratory muscle systems: severe generalized hypotonia is clinically established, but its quantitative contribution to gastric transit is unresolved.
contradictions: The focal report states that delayed gastric emptying was caused by hypotonia, yet it provides no objective gastric-emptying measurement, motility study, or gastric neuromuscular assay; its presented abdominal imaging instead documents colonic stool burden.

The same child presented with enterovirus infection, pneumonia, projectile bilious vomiting, constipation, gastrostomy feeding, dehydration, and medication exposures, all of which complicate attribution of acute gastrointestinal symptoms to a chronic gastric-emptying defect.

The primary ICC experiment found that NALCN was not required for basal pacemaking, contradicting a strong version of the hypothesis that UNC80/NALCN dysfunction necessarily abolishes gastrointestinal slow waves; it supported only partial involvement in substance-P-evoked modulation.
Molecularly defined UNC80 cohorts repeatedly report constipation, reflux, feeding difficulty, and growth failure, but do not independently replicate objectively delayed gastric emptying.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Neuromuscular tone and coordinated propulsive activity are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.causal_level: whole-body neuromuscular state influencing organ-level motility
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: generalized neuromuscular system and gastrointestinal motor apparatus
distinct_mechanisms.label: Generalized hypotonia-associated gastrointestinal propulsion deficit
limitations: The source authors attributed delayed emptying to hypotonia without gastric manometry, emptying measurement, muscle histology, or enteric-neural testing.
Generalized skeletal hypotonia does not by itself identify the gastric cellular lesion.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Adequate axial, abdominal, enteric-neuromuscular, and gastrointestinal smooth-muscle coordination supports feeding and propulsion through the upper gastrointestinal tract.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Severe persistent hypotonia and impaired muscle coordination are proposed to reduce gastrointestinal propulsion, including gastric transit, in UNC80 deficiency.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Proposed upstream contributor to the focal delayed gastric-emptying state; it is not synonymous with gastric transit and is already curated as a separate systemic phenotype.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Modulated depolarizing sodium current and neuropeptide-evoked pacemaker response are inferred to be reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.causal_level: cellular electrophysiology and gastrointestinal pacemaker modulation
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: interstitial cells of Cajal and coupled smooth muscle in the gastrointestinal neuromuscular apparatus
distinct_mechanisms.label: Reduced NALCN-dependent modulation of interstitial-cell-of-Cajal pacemaking
limitations: No UNC80-deficient human gastric interstitial cells of Cajal, enteric neurons, organoids, or motility preparations were studied.
The intestinal-cell experiment used neonatal mouse small-intestinal ICCs, not human gastric ICCs.
NALCN loss spared basal pacemaking and specifically reduced substance-P-evoked modulation, so the evidence does not establish a constitutive pacemaker failure.
The tested UNC80 missense variant-current defect in HEK293T cells cannot be assumed for every biallelic UNC80 genotype.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: NALCN contributes to substance-P-evoked depolarization and modulation of pacemaker currents in intestinal interstitial cells of Cajal, whose slow waves propagate to coupled smooth muscle.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: A reduction in functional UNC80-NALCN current could blunt neuropeptide-dependent pacemaker modulation and thereby reduce coordinated gastrointestinal motor output.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Plausible proximal mechanism for slowed gastric transit, synthesized from separate UNC80 variant-current and mouse intestinal NALCN experiments; absent from the curated node index.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Distal intestinal and colonic transit are reduced.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: small intestine and colon
distinct_mechanisms.label: Co-occurring severe constipation and distal intestinal dysmotility
limitations: Constipation does not demonstrate delayed gastric emptying and may arise through different neural, muscular, dietary, hydration, immobility, or medication mechanisms.
No segmental transit testing was reported in the focal child.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Coordinated intestinal and colonic propulsion produces regular stool transit independently of the rate at which the stomach empties.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Severe constipation and stool retention recur in UNC80-deficient individuals and were prominent during the focal child's admission.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A sibling gastrointestinal dysmotility feature that supports a broader motility phenotype but cannot serve as a surrogate measure of gastric emptying; already indexed separately.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Retention and intolerance are increased when gastric transit is slowed.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract during acute infection
distinct_mechanisms.label: Feeding intolerance and prolonged vomiting vulnerability during acute gastrointestinal illness
limitations: The acute emesis could reflect enterovirus infection, constipation, intercurrent illness, or other factors; delayed emptying was not measured during the episode.
The claim that delayed emptying prolonged infection recovery was an author inference without a comparator or viral-clearance measurement.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Timely gastric transit limits retention and supports tolerance of enteral intake during recovery from an acute gastrointestinal illness.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: The focal child developed projectile bilious emesis during enterovirus infection, and the authors inferred that delayed emptying made recovery more difficult.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Downstream focal detail rather than a separate curated pathology identity.

downstream_consequences: Feeding intolerance and dependence on gastrostomy feeding may be aggravated by slow upper-gastrointestinal transit, although oral-motor dysfunction and global disability are independent contributors.
Poor weight gain and failure to thrive may be aggravated by gastrointestinal dysfunction but are multifactorial in UNC80 deficiency.
Vomiting and difficulty tolerating acute gastroenteritis were attributed by the case authors to delayed emptying, without objective transit or recovery measurements.
Constipation and distal stool retention co-occur but should not be represented as consequences of gastric emptying without segmental transit evidence.
Aspiration risk could plausibly increase with gastric retention and reflux, but no direct gastric-emptying-to-aspiration link was demonstrated in the focal case.

established_pathology_observations.observation: Delayed gastric emptying was explicitly reported in a three-year-old child labelled as having UNC80 disease and severe hypotonia.

Four individuals with pathogenic biallelic UNC80 variants had severe constipation, and a later child with a homozygous UNC80 nonsense variant had severe constipation and reflux, establishing broader gastrointestinal dysfunction without specifically measuring gastric emptying.
A disease-associated UNC80 missense construct produced significantly smaller NALCN currents than wild-type UNC80 in transfected HEK293T cells.
NALCN knockout reduced substance-P-evoked depolarization and inward current in cultured neonatal mouse small-intestinal interstitial cells of Cajal, while basal pacemaking persisted.

gaps: Replication of delayed gastric emptying in additional people with molecularly confirmed biallelic UNC80 variants.
Objective measurement of solid and liquid gastric emptying with age-appropriate normative comparison and exclusion of mechanical obstruction.

Genotype clarification for the focal child, because the report describes a large homozygous chromosomal region rather than a specific biallelic UNC80 variant and does not exclude contribution from other genes in that interval.
Direct study of human gastric interstitial cells of Cajal, enteric neurons, smooth muscle, or patient-derived gastrointestinal models carrying UNC80 variants.
Separation of gastric transit from oral-motor dysfunction, reflux, constipation, tube-feeding regimen, immobility, intercurrent infection, hydration, and medication effects.

Determination of whether the relevant channel defect affects basal slow waves, neuropeptide modulation, autonomic input, pyloric coordination, antral contractility, accommodation, or a combination of these processes.
Longitudinal data defining age of onset, persistence, severity, nutritional consequences, aspiration relationship, and within-person variability.
mechanisms: Generalized hypotonia and impaired neuromuscular coordination were proposed by the case authors to reduce gastrointestinal propulsion; disease cohorts independently confirm severe hypotonia and constipation but not the gastric-specific step.

UNC80 supports NALCN-channel function. A pathogenic UNC80 missense construct retained detectable binding to channel-complex partners yet produced significantly reduced NALCN currents in HEK293T cells, showing a functional channel defect for that variant.

In neonatal mouse small-intestinal interstitial cells of Cajal, NALCN contributes to substance-P/Src-dependent depolarization and inward current that modulate pacemaking. NALCN knockout did not abolish basal pacemaking, arguing against a simple requirement for NALCN in all gastrointestinal slow-wave generation.

Severe constipation and reflux recur across molecularly defined UNC80 cases, supporting broader gastrointestinal dysmotility as part of the disease spectrum while remaining anatomically and physiologically distinct from gastric emptying.
profiles.normal_state: Normal gastric emptying depends on coordinated accommodation, antral propulsion, pyloric opening, duodenal resistance, and enteric neuromuscular timing. Interstitial cells of Cajal generate and propagate electrical slow waves to coupled gastrointestinal smooth muscle, supporting rhythmic phasic contractions; the NALCN channel contributes to substance-P-evoked modulation of this pacemaker activity in cultured neonatal mouse small-intestinal cells, but is not required for their basal pacemaking.
profiles.pathological_state: The focal abnormal state is slowed transfer of gastric contents from the stomach in an affected child. In the only direct UNC80-disease report, delayed gastric emptying was asserted as a manifestation of hypotonia, alongside G-tube dependence, poor weight gain, severe constipation, vomiting during acute enterovirus infection, and respiratory disease. No gastric scintigraphy, breath test, wireless motility measurement, antroduodenal manometry, or exclusion of mechanical gastric-outlet obstruction was reported, so the abnormal transit state remains a case-level clinical attribution rather than a quantified phenotype.
profiles.summary: Delayed gastric emptying is reported as a baseline gastrointestinal dysfunction in one three-year-old child labelled as having UNC80 disease. The disease-specific observation is clinically plausible within a broader pattern of severe hypotonia, feeding dependence, constipation, reflux, and growth failure, but it was not documented by an objective gastric-emptying assay. A mechanistic connection to the NALCN channelosome can be synthesized from separate experiments showing that a disease-associated UNC80 variant reduces NALCN current and that NALCN participates in neuropeptide-evoked modulation of murine intestinal interstitial-cell-of-Cajal pacemaking; this cross-model connection is inferred and is not demonstrated in the affected child's stomach.
temporal_context: Delayed gastric emptying was described as a baseline dysfunction before or during presentation at age three years, but onset and persistence were not reported.
Projectile bilious emesis and impaired recovery were observed during an acute enterovirus gastroenteritis and pneumonia admission.
Severe hypotonia, feeding dependence, and poor weight gain were chronic developmental features.
The cellular pacemaker evidence derives from mice within approximately 24 hours of birth and one day of ICC culture, limiting developmental transfer.
profiles.uncertainty: Confidence is moderate that broader gastrointestinal dysmotility belongs to the UNC80-deficiency spectrum, because severe constipation and reflux recur in molecularly defined cases. Confidence is low that delayed gastric emptying itself is a general disease feature: it is directly asserted in only one case, lacks an objective emptying test, and the reported genotype is incompletely specified. The ICC mechanism is biologically coherent but remains a cross-species, cross-compartment synthesis. The direction of the synthesis follows from reduced NALCN current with one pathogenic UNC80 variant and reduced substance-P-evoked ICC depolarization after Nalcn loss; neither experiment establishes gastric dysmotility in a person with UNC80 deficiency.
upstream_causes: A clinical UNC80-disease label in the focal case, described as a large 44 Mb homozygous region on chromosome 2 rather than a fully specified causal UNC80 variant.
Severe generalized hypotonia and impaired gastrointestinal muscle coordination, proposed by the focal case authors.
Reduced functional output of the UNC80-NALCN channel complex, directly demonstrated for one disease-associated UNC80 missense construct in a heterologous-cell assay.
Possible impairment of NALCN-dependent neuropeptide modulation in gastrointestinal pacemaker cells, an inference not tested in the disease.

anatomical_context: oral cavity and oropharynx for bolus containment and propulsion
pharynx and laryngeal vestibule for airway closure and residue clearance
proximal tracheobronchial tree as the site of recurrent airway entry
lung parenchyma as the site of aspiration-associated pneumonia
respiratory musculature and cough apparatus as modifiers of retained airway burden
profiles.causal_role: Recurrent aspiration is positioned as a proximal airway-exposure event downstream of impaired swallowing and airway protection and upstream of possible airway obstruction, inflammatory lung injury, pneumonia, and respiratory decompensation. This ordering is a mechanistic inference from the reported aspiration and established swallowing biology. It does not establish that aspiration causes every respiratory infection in UNC80 deficiency, because infection also depends on aspirate composition, pathogen burden, cough and secretion clearance, pulmonary reserve, and host susceptibility.
cell_types: cranial and brainstem swallowing-network neurons, inferred but not assayed in UNC80 aspiration cases
oropharyngeal and laryngeal skeletal muscle fibers, inferred from swallowing biomechanics and hypotonia
laryngeal sensory and cough-reflex afferent neurons, relevant to silent aspiration but untested in UNC80 deficiency
airway epithelial and innate immune cells, downstream responders in aspiration-associated lung injury and infection but not profiled in UNC80 cases
contradictions: The focal observation is replicated only indirectly by a later report of aspiration pneumonia; neither report provides instrumental confirmation, so the exact airway-invasion mechanism remains unresolved.
Documented tracheal aspiration does not invariably progress to pneumonia: a pediatric cerebral-palsy study observed no post-study pneumonia in 32 children with tracheal aspiration.

A separate UNC80-associated case had enterovirus pneumonia and impaired secretion clearance without demonstrated aspiration, showing that respiratory disease in this population can arise through non-aspiration or mixed routes.
The secretion-clearance case involved a large homozygous chromosomal interval, limiting gene-specific causal attribution.
No evidence located here establishes primary immune dysfunction, but absence of such evidence does not prove that all infections are secondary to aspiration or hypotonia.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Oropharyngeal coordination and airway protection are reduced, increasing airway invasion.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: oral cavity, pharynx, hyoid-laryngeal complex, and laryngeal vestibule
distinct_mechanisms.label: Oropharyngeal swallowing-kinematic and airway-closure failure
limitations: The UNC80 reports document aspiration or aspiration pneumonia but do not identify the failed swallow phase or kinematic event.
The detailed kinematic evidence comes from general human swallowing physiology and an infant-pig lesion model, not from UNC80-deficient participants.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Coordinated tongue, hyoid, laryngeal, and pharyngeal movements contain and propel the bolus while closing and displacing the airway out of its path.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Disordered oral-pharyngeal timing or inadequate laryngeal closure permits penetration and aspiration during feeding or swallowing.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: Plausible upstream generator of recurrent aspiration; this is an inference because UNC80-specific instrumental swallowing physiology has not been reported.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Post-swallow residue and subsequent airway entry are increased.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: pharynx, laryngeal inlet, and proximal trachea
distinct_mechanisms.label: Post-swallow aspiration of retained pharyngeal material
limitations: No retained residue, timing of aspiration, or aspirate source has been measured in an UNC80-deficient individual.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Pharyngeal residue is cleared before respiration resumes, preventing retained material from being inhaled.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Material retained after a swallow remains available to enter the airway when breathing resumes.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A mechanistically distinct timing route contained within the focal recurrent-aspiration identity.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Detectability of aspiration by symptoms is reduced despite persistent airway invasion.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: oropharyngeal-laryngeal sensory and cough-reflex apparatus
distinct_mechanisms.label: Silent airway invasion
limitations: Silent aspiration is documented in pediatric dysphagia populations, not specifically in UNC80 deficiency.
No videofluoroscopic or endoscopic swallowing study was reported in the UNC80 cases retained here.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Airway invasion elicits observable protective responses such as cough or choking that signal impaired swallowing.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Material enters the airway without overt cough, choking, or other clinical signs, allowing repeated events to go unrecognized.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A focal-detail presentation that could conceal recurrence but has not been tested in UNC80 deficiency.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Lower-airway infection burden and systemic infectious deterioration are increased after aspiration-associated exposure.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: tracheobronchial tree, lung parenchyma, and systemic inflammatory circulation
distinct_mechanisms.label: Aspiration-associated pneumonia and septic deterioration
limitations: The original recurrent-aspiration report did not establish that the individual's respiratory infections were aspiration-mediated.
The later aspiration-pneumonia report is one family case and provides no microbiology, swallow study, or exposure-frequency data.
A pediatric cerebral-palsy cohort had no immediate pneumonia despite documented tracheal aspiration in 32 children, demonstrating that the progression is non-deterministic.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Lower airways remain protected from repeated inoculation and maintain sufficient local clearance and host defense to avoid infection.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Aspiration-associated lower-airway disease progresses to pneumonia and, in a severe reported UNC80 case, septic shock and death.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: A clinically important downstream consequence of the focal aspiration event; aspiration alone is not sufficient to determine whether pneumonia follows.

distinct_mechanisms.biological_direction: Respiratory secretion clearance is reduced and retained airway burden is increased.
distinct_mechanisms.compartment: airways and respiratory musculature
distinct_mechanisms.label: Hypotonia-associated respiratory secretion-clearance failure
limitations: The supporting child carried a reported 44 Mb homozygous interval, so attribution to UNC80 alone is confounded.
The report did not instrumentally demonstrate aspiration or quantify cough and secretion clearance.
distinct_mechanisms.normal_state: Effective respiratory muscle force and cough clear airway secretions and reduce retained material after airway exposure.
distinct_mechanisms.pathological_state: Severe hypotonia impairs secretion clearance, promoting retained secretions and pneumonia risk independently of whether aspiration initiated the exposure.
distinct_mechanisms.relationship_to_focal: An indexed parallel and downstream modifier that may magnify the pulmonary consequences of recurrent aspiration but does not establish aspiration frequency.

downstream_consequences: repeated tracheobronchial exposure to food, liquid, saliva, or refluxate
possible silent, cumulative airway injury without overt choking or cough
aspiration-associated pneumonia and severe respiratory decompensation
septic shock and death in one later reported affected individual
interaction with hypotonia-associated secretion-clearance failure and limited pulmonary reserve
respiratory infection cannot be assigned to aspiration without event-linked pulmonary evidence

established_pathology_observations.observation: An individual with biallelic UNC80-associated severe infantile encephalopathy had a history of recurrent aspiration.

A later UNC80-related family case developed severe aspiration pneumonia and then septic shock and death, independently confirming that aspiration-associated lower-airway disease can occur in this disorder.

A child described as having an UNC80 mutation had recurrent pneumonia and an inability to clear respiratory secretions attributed by the authors to hypotonia; aspiration itself was not demonstrated in that case.

gaps: Prevalence and recurrence rate of aspiration across UNC80 genotypes, ages, and disease severities are unknown.
No UNC80-specific videofluoroscopic swallow study, fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation, salivagram, or event-linked airway sampling was identified.
The aspirated material, consistency, volume, timing within the swallow, and silent-versus-symptomatic status are unknown.
The relative contributions of oral-motor dysfunction, generalized hypotonia, seizures, alertness, sleep-state abnormalities, reflux, and delayed gastric emptying have not been separated.
